I.A. Human Behavior and Eﬀec3ve Communica3on 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Years of thinking people have understood you. Unless you’ve known this stuﬀ, they haven’t.  
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Basic human needs as well as defense mechanisms and eﬀec3ve communica3on. 
Why 
Learning is a change of behavior as a result of experience. To successfully accomplish the task of helping bring 
about this change, the instructor must know why people act the way they do. 
How: 
1.Deﬁni8ons of Human Behavior 
A.The study of human behavior is an amempt to explain how and why human func3ons the way they do 
i.Combo of innate human nature and individual experience & environment 
B.Scien3ﬁc World Deﬁni3on 
i.Product of factors that cause people to act in predictable ways 
a.Ex: how people handle fear is a product of individual experiences 
•Public speaking example in Avia3on Instructor’s Handbook 
C.Sa3sfying Needs Deﬁni3on 
i.Human behavior is the result of amempts to sa3sfy certain needs 
a.Simple needs may drive behavior: food, water 
b.Also may be driven by complex needs: respect and acceptance 
ii.To a large extent thoughts, feelings and behavior are shared by all men and women 
D.Life Course of Humans Deﬁni3on 
i.As humans grow, behavior changes 
a.As an individual matures, their mode of ac3ons moves from dependency to self-direc3on 
b.Therefore, the age of the learner impacts how the curriculum is designed 
E.Personality Types 
i.Myers Briggs Type Indicator 
a.Seeming random varia3on in human behavior is quite structured due to diﬀerences in way 
individuals prefer to use their percep3on & judgment  
ii.Now used to discover future careers 
F.Instructor and Learner Rela3onship 
i.Instructor must understand his/her style of teaching and as much as possible adapt to learners 
a.Adjust scenarios to ﬁt learner’s learning  
G.Control of Human Behavior 
i.Learners tend to submit to authority as a valid means of control 
a.The instructor’s challenge is to know what controls are best for exis3ng circumstances 
b.Create an atmosphere that enables/encourages learners to help themselves toward their goals 
ii.It is the instructor’s responsibility to discover how to realize the poten3al in each learner 
a.See the mo3va3on and human nature generaliza3ons (pg. 2-1)

iii.How to mold a solid/healthy/produc3ve rela3onship depends on the instructor’s knowledge of

H.A working knowledge of behavior can help an instructor bemer understand a learner 
2.Human Needs and Mo8va8on 
A.Hierarchy of Human Needs – An organiza3on of human needs into levels of importance 
i.Un3l the needs are sa3sﬁed, one can’t focus fully on learning, self-expression, or any other task 
a.Once a need is sa3sﬁed, it no longer provides mo3va3on

C.Security 
i.Protec3on against danger, threats, depriva3on 
aﬀect learner behavior 
ii.If a learner does not feel safe, he or she cannot

D.Belonging

b.Externally - Rela3ng to reputa3on: status, recogni3on, apprecia3on, and respect of associates

iii.Aesthe3c: Emo3onal needs

G.Self-Actualiza8on 
i.When all other needs are sa3sﬁed only then can self-actualiza3on be amained

ii.Realizing one’s own poten3al for con3nued development/Reaching personal goals & poten3al 
H.Help learners sa3sfy their own needs in a manner that will create a healthy learning environment 
3.Defense Mechanisms 
A.Subconscious, almost automa3c, ego-protec3ng reac3ons to unpleasant situa3ons

I.A. Human Behavior and Eﬀec3ve Communica3on 
i.A person places uncomfortable thoughts into inaccessible areas of the unconscious mind. Things a 
person is unable to cope with now are pushed away, to be dealt with at another 3me, or hopefully 
never because they fade away on their own accord 
C.Denial 
i.Refusal to accept a reality because it is too threatening 
D.Compensa8on 
i.Learners amempt to disguise the presence of a weak quality by emphasizing a more posi3ve one 
a.“I’m not a ﬁghter, I’m a lover” philosophy can be an example of compensa3on 
ii.May accept and develop a less preferred but more amainable objec3ve instead of a more preferred 
but less amainable objec3ve 
E.Projec8on 
i.Blame is relegated to others for their own shortcomings, mistakes, and transgressions 
ii.Mo3ves, desires, characteris3cs, and impulses are amributed to others 
iii.“I failed because I had a poor examiner” – the learner believes the failure was not their fault 
F.Ra8onaliza8on 
i.Subconscious technique for jus3fying ac3ons that otherwise would be unacceptable 
ii.When true ra3onaliza3on takes place, individuals sincerely believe in their excuses 
iii.For example, failing a test because “there was not enough 3me to study,” when the learner skipped 
study groups and prac3ce tests 
G.Reac8on Forma8on 
i.Some3mes individuals protect themselves from dangerous desires by not only repressing them, but 
actually developing conscious aptudes and behavior pamerns that are just the opposite 
H.Fantasy 
i.Daydreaming about how things should be rather than doing something about how they are 
I.Displacement 
i.Unconscious shib of emo3on, aﬀect, or desire from the original object to a more acceptable, less 
threatening subs3tute 
4.Learner Emo8onal Reac8ons 
A.Anxiety – “A state of mental uneasiness arising from fear…” 
i.Most signiﬁcant psychological factor aﬀec3ng ﬂight instruc3on 
ii.Anxiety can be countered by reinforcing enjoyment of ﬂying, and by teaching to cope with fear 
a.Treat fears as a normal reac3on, do not ignore them 
iii.Introduce maneuvers with care so the learner knows what to expect/what their reac3on should be 
B.Impa3ence 
i.An impa3ent learner fails to understand the need for preliminary training and seeks only the 
ul3mate objec3ve without considering the means to reach it 
ii.Counter impa3ence by presen3ng the necessary preliminary training one step at a 3me, with clearly 
state goals for each step, while tailing instruc3on to the pace of the learner (i.e. slow learner vs 
mo3vated, fast learner) 
C.Worry or Lack of Interest 
i.Learners who are worried or emo3onally upset are not ready to learn and derive limle beneﬁt from 
instruc3on 
a.Outside experiences aﬀect behavior and performance in training – the instructor is not 
responsible for these diversions, but also cannot ignore them because they aﬀect learning 
ii.Instruc3on should be keyed to divert amen3on from their worries and troubles to the tasks at hand 
iii.The most eﬀec3ve cure is preven3on – ensure the learner knows at the end of each lesson exactly 
how well they have progressed and what deﬁciencies are present 
D.Physical Discomfort, Illness, Fa3gue, and Dehydra3on 
i.All of these condi3ons slow the rate of learning, and should be mi3gated to the extent possible 
ii.Fa3gue – one of the most treacherous hazards to ﬂight safety

I.A. Human Behavior and Eﬀec3ve Communica3on 
a.Acute Fa3gue: Normal occurrence of everyday living 
b.Chronic Fa3gue: Combina3on of both physiological problems and psychological issues (ﬁnancial, 
home life, job-related stress) 
c.Fa3gue impairs and adversely aﬀects pilot judgement and decision making  
d.Be aware of fa3gue and adjust the length and frequency of training as necessary 
iii.Dehydra3on and Heatstroke 
a.Dehydra3on: Cri3cal loss of water to the body. Reduces alertness 
b.Heatstroke: Inability of the body to control its temperature 
c.Carry ample water on any long ﬂight, keep the temperature cool, and wear light clothing 
E.Apathy Due to Inadequate Instruc3on 
i.To hold interest and maintain mo3va3on, provide well-planned, appropriate and accurate instruc3on 
ii.Instruc3on should be meaningful. Teach to the level of the learner . Be professional (appearance and 
presenta3on of material) 
iii.Once the instructor loses conﬁdence, it is diﬃcult to regain and learning is diminished  
F.Normal Reac3ons to Stress 
i.Respond rapidly and exactly, within the limits of their experience and training 
a.This is desired, stress should not overwhelm and cause abnormal reac3ons (below) 
G.Abnormal Reac3ons to Stress 
i.Response may be completely absent or at least inadequate 
ii.Response may be random or illogical, or they may do more than is called for by the situa3on 
iii.Abnormal Reac3ons:  
a.Inappropriate reac3on, such as extreme over-coopera3on, painstaking self-control, 
inappropriate laughter or singing, and very rapid changes in emo3on 
b.Marked changes in mood on diﬀerent lessons (excellent morale/deep depression) 
c.Severe anger to the instructor, service personnel, and others 
H.Flight Instructors Ac3ons Regarding Seriously Abnormal Learners 
i.Refrain from instruc3ng the learner and assure they don’t con3nue training/become cer3ﬁcated 
ii.This is done by: 
a.Arranging for another instructor (not acquainted with the learner) to conduct an evalua3on 
ﬂight. Aber the ﬂight, the two instructors should confer to determine whether they agree that 
further inves3ga3on or ac3on is jus3ﬁed  
b.The instructor’s primary legal responsibility concerns the decision whether to endorse the 
learner to for solo, or recommend for the prac3cal test. If, aber consulta3on with an unbiased 
instructor, the instructor believes that the learner may have a serious psychological deﬁciency, 
the endorsements/recommenda3on should be withheld  
5.Basic Elements of Communica8on 
A.A style of communica3on must be developed that can convey info to learners 
B.Basic Elements 
i.Communica3on takes place when a person transmits ideas/feelings to another 
ii.Eﬀec3veness is measured by the similarity between the idea transmimed and the idea received 
a.Receiver reacts with understanding and changes their behavior accordingly 
b.A change in behavior is the goal of communica3on 
iii.3 elements of communica3on: The Source, The Symbols, The Receiver 
iv.The Source (the sender, speaker, transmimer, or instructor) 
a.Eﬀec3veness as a communicator is related to 3 basic factors 
•An ability to select and use language is essen3al for transmipng meaningful symbols 
a.Eﬀec3veness of communica3on is dependent on the understanding of the words used 
b.Basically, the words you use are important to learning 
•Communicators reveal informa3on about themselves – self-image, views of ideas being 
communicated as well as the receiver

6.Barriers to Eﬀec8ve Communica8on 
A.Lack of Common Experience 
i.Greatest single barrier to eﬀec3ve communica3on 
ii.A communicator’s words cannot communicate the desired meaning to another person unless he has 
had some experience with the objects or concepts to which these words refer 
a.It is essen3al that instructors speak the same language as the learners 
b.If speciﬁc terminology is needed, ensure understanding (especially common in avia3on) 
B.Confusion Between the Symbol and the Symbolized Object 
i.This results when a word is confused with what it is meant to represent 
a.Words and symbols do not always represent the same thing to every person 
b.Make sure associa3ons are clear 
ii.For communica3on to be eﬀec3ve, the learner’s understanding must match the instructor’s 
C.Overuse of Abstrac3ons (Abstrac3ons are words that are general rather than speciﬁc) 
i.The danger is that abstrac3ons do not evoke the same items of experience in the minds of learners 
a.Avoid abstrac3ons in most cases 
D.External Factors 
i.Factors outside the instructor’s control that prevent a process or ac3vity from being carried out 
properly (physiological, environmental, psychological elements) 
ii.Physiological interference is any physical problem that may inhibit understanding 
a.Hearing loss, injury, physical illness, etc. 
iii.Environmental interference is caused by external physical condi3ons (like noise) 
iv.Psychological interference is a product of how the learner/instructor feel 
a.If either isn’t commimed, or if fear or mistrust exist, then communica3on is impaired 
v.Consider the eﬀects of these factors and mi3gate them where possible 
E.Interference 
i.Occurs when the message gets disrupted, truncated, or added to somewhere in the communica3on 
sequence 
a.While the instructor/learner may believe an intact message was sent/received, that may be 
inaccurate  
ii.Addi3onal feedback and conﬁrma3on reduce the harmful eﬀects of interference

Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Understanding how people learn, and applying that knowledge to the learning environment. 
Why 
As a ﬂight instructor, the ability to eﬀec3vely teach learners is impera3ve. Understanding how people learn 
and how to apply that knowledge is the basis for eﬀec3ve teaching. 
How: 
1.Learning Theory 
A.Deﬁni3on – A body of principles used to explain how people acquire skills, knowledge, and aptudes 
B.How people learn is explained by 2 basic concepts: Behaviorism and Cogni3ve Theory 
C.Behaviorism (Posi3ve Reinforcement, rather than no reinforcement or punishment) 
i.Stresses the importance of having par3cular behavior reinforced, to shape or control what is learned 
a.The instructor provides the reinforcement 
ii.Frequent posi3ve reinforcement and rewards accelerate learning 
iii.The theory provides ways to encourage the learner’s progress and learning with rewards 
iv.Today, behaviorism is used more to break unwanted behaviors, such as smoking, than in teaching 
a.The popularity of behaviorism has waned – learning has been shown to be a much more 
complex process than a response to a s3muli 
D.Cogni3ve Theory (Focuses on what is going on inside the learner’s mind) 
i.Learning isn’t just a change in behavior; it is a change in the way a learner thinks/understands/feels 
ii.Two Major Branches of the Cogni3ve Theory 
a.The Informa3on Processing Theory 
•The learner’s brain has internal structures which select and process incoming material, 
store/retrieve it, use it to produce behavior, and receive/process feedback on the results 
a.This involves a number of cogni3ve processes: gathering and represen3ng informa3on 
(encoding), retaining of informa3on, and retrieving the informa3on when needed 
b.The brain gets input from the senses (sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell); the amount of 
sensory input the brain receives per second is incredibly high, so the brain will let many 
of the habitual and rou3ne things go unno3ced 
1.For example, a pilot using rudder when entering a turn is oben unaware of pressing 
the pedal 
2.The human unconscious takes charge, leaving the conscious thought processes free 
b.Construc3vism 
•Learning is the result of the learner matching new informa3on against preexis3ng 
informa3on and integra3ng it into meaningful connec3ons 
a.Learners do not acquire knowledge and skills passively, but ac3vely build or construct 
them based on their experiences

6.Characteris8cs of Learning (PRMA) 
A.To be eﬀec3ve, the learning situa3on should be purposeful, based on experience, mul3faceted, and

B.Purposeful 
i.In the process of learning, the learner’s goals are the most important factor

ii.Capable of retaining informa3on for only a very short period of 3me and within seconds the relevant

C.Short-Term Memory (Coding, Rehearsal, Recoding) 
i.Short-term memory resembles the control tower of a major airport and is responsible for 
coordina3ng all incoming and outgoing ﬂights 
a.Informa3on is stored for roughly 30 seconds, aber which it may rapidly fade or be consolidated 
into long-term memory, depending on the individual’s priori3es

a.The sor3ng process is called Coding or Chunking 
b.Usually takes 5 - 10 sec; if interrupted, the informa3on is easily lost since it is only stored for 30 
seconds 
iii.Time limited and Capacity limited (3me limita3on can be overcome by repe33on) 
iv.The coding process may involve recoding to adjust informa3on to individual experiences  
a.This is when actual learning begins to take place 
b.Recoding: rela3ng incoming informa3on to concepts or knowledge already in memory 
v.Three basic opera3ons of Short-term memory 
a.Iconic Memory: Brief sensory memory of visual images 
b.Acous3c Memory: Encoded memory of a brief sound memory or the ability to hold sounds in 
short-term memory 
c.Working Memory: Ac3ve process to keep informa3on un3l it is put to use

vi.Developing a logical strategy for coding informa3on is a signiﬁcant step in the learning process

F.Forgepng 
i.There are many theories regarding why people forget (FIIRS)

I.G. Risk Management 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
We’re pilots, we like the rush of ﬂight and the sense of danger .  All FAA opera3ons in the United States involve 
risk; don’t let the risk and danger get out of control. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Risk management is a decision-making process designed to perceive hazards systema3cally, assess the degree 
of risk associated with a hazard, and determine the best course of ac3on. 
Why 
Flying is inherently dangerous, but there are ways to keep the danger to a minimum. This lesson will describe 
ways to recognize and mi3gate the risk involved with ﬂying. 
How: 
1.Principles of Risk Management 
A.The goal of risk management is to proac3vely iden3fy safety-related hazards and mi3gate the associated 
risks 
B.Accept no Unnecessary Risk 
i.Only accept the necessary risk 
a.Flying is impossible without risk, do not make a situa3on more dangerous than necessary 
C.Make Risk Decisions at the Appropriate Level 
i.In single pilot situa3ons, the pilot makes decisions (not ATC, or passengers) 
ii.In other situa3ons, it may be beneﬁcial to “go up the ladder” for a decision 
a.i.e. Talk to the chief pilot or experienced CFI about a poten3ally risky situa3on 
D.Accept Risk When Beneﬁts Outweigh the Costs 
i.Analyze costs and beneﬁts, make an informed decision 
E.Integrate Risk Management into Planning at All Levels 
i.Safety requires risk management planning in all stages of ﬂight 
a.Plan early and throughout to avoid unnecessary, ampliﬁed risk 
2.Risk Management Process 
A.Step 1: Iden3fy the Hazard 
i.A hazard is any real or poten3al condi3on that can cause degrada3on, injury, illness, death, damage 
to or loss of equipment or property 
B.Step 2: Assess the Risk 
i.Determine the level of risk associated with the iden3ﬁed hazards 
a.Assess in terms of its likelihood (probability) and its severity (consequences) 
ii.Develop a method to tangibly measure risk (Risk Assessment Matrix, below) 
C.Step 3: Mi3gate the Risk 
i.Look into ways to reduce, mi3gate, or eliminate the risk 
ii.All risks have 2 components: Probability of occurrence & Severity of the hazard 
a.Try to reduce or eliminate at least one component 
iii.Use the Cost/Beneﬁt analysis to decide if it is worth accep3ng the risk 
3.Level of Risk 
A.The level of risk posed by a given hazard is measured in terms of:  
55

I.G. Risk Management 
i. Severity (extent of possible loss)  
ii. Probability (likelihood that a hazard will cause a loss) 
4.Assessing Risk 
A.Pilots must diﬀeren3ate in advance between a low-risk ﬂight and a high-risk ﬂight 
B.Establish a review process and develop strategies to minimize risk on the high and low risk ﬂights 
C.The Risk Matrix is a helpful risk assessment model 
i.Assesses the likelihood of an event occurring and the consequences of that event 
a.Likelihood (probability of occurrence): Probable, Occasional, Remote, Improbable 
•i.e. Likelihood of a pilot ﬂying MVFR to encounter IFR condi3ons 
b.Severity: Catastrophic, Cri3cal, Marginal, Negligible

ii.High Probability/Severity is bad and vice versa: 
5.Mi8ga8ng Risk 
A.Aber determining the level of risk, the pilot needs to reduce the risk  
i.Analyze op3ons that can reduce unnecessary risk 
a.i.e. Cancel/delay ﬂight, bring CFI or more experienced pilot, etc. 
B.By eﬀec3vely mi3ga3ng known risks to acceptable levels, pilots can complete their planned ﬂights safely 
or ensure alternate op3ons are selected for those rare occasions when the planned or ongoing ﬂight

iii.Stress – Family, money, rela3onships, work, etc.

7.PAVE Checklist 
A.Another way to mi3gate risk 
B.The risks of ﬂight are divided into 4 categories

Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story

What

Why

How:

•Know of any medical condi3on that would prevent you from obtaining a medical

a.It’s the pilot’s judgment (be safe, and conserva3ve)

Overview

What

aircrab movement on the airport surface while reducing the risk of runway incursions. 
Why 
Runway incursions have some3mes led to serious accidents with signiﬁcant loss of aircrab as well as life.

Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
AC90-48C Appendix 1: 
How much 3me do you think you would have to react if two planes were approaching each other at 360 mph 
from 10 miles out? 100 seconds 
How about from 4 miles? 40 seconds 
1 mile? 10 seconds 
½ Mile? 5 seconds 
What if the planes were approaching at 600 MPH? 12 seconds from 2 miles; 3 seconds from ½ mile 
You can see that it’s very important that we look out for other traﬃc. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Visual scanning and collision avoidance is the ability to eﬀec3vely scan the sky for poten3al collision threats.   
Why 
Safety. Visual scanning and collision avoidance is very important in crea3ng safe skies. A diligent visual scan to 
avoid collision threats is paramount to the safety of all pilots. 
How: 
1.“See and Avoid” (FAR 91.113, AC 90-48) 
A.Flight rules prescribed in FAR part 91 set forth the concept of “See and Avoid” 
B.The Concept 
i.Vigilance shall be maintained at all 3mes, by each person opera3ng an aircrab, regardless of whether 
the opera3on is conducted under IFR or VFR 
ii.Although the task of avoiding other aircrab is oben a shared job, the pilot is always responsible to 
see and avoid traﬃc (never rely en3rely on ATC for collision avoidance) 
2.Proper Visual Scanning (AIM 8-1-6) 
A.Remain constantly alert to all traﬃc movement within the ﬁeld of vision, as well as periodically scanning 
the en3re visual ﬁeld to ensure detec3on of conﬂic3ng traﬃc 
B.Eﬀec3ve scanning 
i.At one glance, only a very small area called the fovea, has the ability to send a clear, sharply focused 
image to the brain (center of vision) 
a.This is during daylight, at night, vision works diﬀerently 
b.All other visual informa3on not processed directly through the fovea will be of less detail 
ii.To scan eﬀec3vely, use short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas of the sky in 
the central visual ﬁeld 
a.Each movement should not exceed 10o and each area should be observed for at least 1 second 
iii.Peripheral Vision 
a.Can be very useful in spopng collision threats 
•Apparent movement is oben detected by the peripherals 
b.Visual search at night depends almost en3rely on the peripherals 
•The fovea is very good in the daylight, but doesn’t see well at night, your peripheral vision is 
much bemer at night and thus is primary in detec3ng traﬃc in the dark

and the path of least resistance is the 3ps of the

3ps

a.These vor3ces increase drag because of energy 
spent in producing the turbulence 
vii.Thus, whenever an airfoil is producing lib, induced

a.Just as lib increases with AOA, induced drag also increases 
b.As AOA increases, there is a greater pressure diﬀerence between the top/bomom of the wing 
•Greater pressure diﬀerence = greater lateral airﬂow and stronger vor3ces 
B.Strength of the Vor3ces 
i.As men3oned, the greater the AOA, the stronger the vor3ces 
a.Therefore, the strongest vor3ces occur when the aircrab is heavy, clean, and slow 
b.Strength is directly propor3onal to weight and inversely propor3onal to wingspan and airspeed

•As airspeed decreases, AOA increases 
ii.Thus, the strongest vor3ces occur during takeoﬀ, climb, and landing 
C.Dangers of Vor3ces 
i.Wake turbulence can be a hazard to any aircrab signiﬁcantly lighter than the genera3ng aircrab 
ii.Flying through another aircrab’s wake can result in major structural damage, or induced rolling 
making the aircrab uncontrollable

downwind vortex 
a.Be cau3ous, this could move another aircrab’s vor3ces into your path

Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What:   
The four forces of ﬂight are in essence the fundamental principles that govern ﬂight; they are what make an 
airplane ﬂy. 
Why:  
How well a pilot performs in ﬂight depends on the ability to plan and coordinate the use of power and ﬂight 
controls to change the forces of thrust, drag, lib, and weight. It is the balance between these forces that the 
pilot must always control. The bemer the understanding of the forces, and means of controlling of them, the 
greater pilot’s skill.  
How: 
1.Intro - Forces of Flight 
A.Lib – The upward force created by the eﬀect of airﬂow as it passes over and under the wing 
B.Weight – Opposes lib, and is caused by the downward pull of gravity 
C.Thrust – The forward force which propels the airplane through the air 
D.Drag – Opposes thrust, and is the backward, or retarding force, which limits the speed of the airplane 
E.Terminology: 
i.Chord Line: The imaginary straight line joining the leading and trailing edges of an airfoil 
ii.Rela3ve Wind:  The direc3on of movement of the wind rela3ve to the aircrab’s ﬂight path. It is 
opposite the aircrab’s ﬂight path, and irrespec3ve of the angle of amack 
a.EX: Straight and level slow ﬂight and high-speed ﬂight have the same rela3ve wind 
iii.Angle of Amack: The angle between the chord line and the rela3ve wind 
2.Lin 
A.The force that opposes weight 
B.Principles of Lib 
i.Newton’s three laws of mo3on: 
a.Newton’s 1st Law: A body at rest tends to remain at rest, and a body in mo3on tends to remain 
moving at the same speed and in the same direc3on 
b.Newton’s 2nd Law: When a body is acted upon by a constant force, its resul3ng accelera3on is 
inversely propor3onal to the mass of the body and is directly propor3onal to the applied force 
•The law may be expressed by the following formula: Force = Mass x Accelera3on (F=ma) 
c.Newton’s 3rd Law: For every ac3on, there is an equal and opposite reac3on 
ii.Bernoulli’s Principle 
a.As the velocity of a ﬂuid (air) increases, its internal pressure decreases 
3.Airfoils 
A.Deﬁni3on 
i.An airfoil is any surface, such as a wing, which provides aerodynamic force when it interacts with a 
moving stream of air

c.A thin layer of air clings to these surfaces and creates small eddies which add to drag 
c.Parasite Drag and Airplane Speed

a.EX: Plane, at a constant al3tude has 4x as the parasite drag at 160 knots than at 80 knots 
d.Main Point: As airspeed increases, Parasite drag increases

certain addi3onal work that is dissipated or lost in the system 
b.The more eﬃcient the system, the smaller the loss 
b.The Wing as a System

a.Induced drag is inherent whenever lib is produced 
c.How it Works

balanced by an increase in the horizontal component of lib

ii.To maintain a constant rate of turn with an increased airspeed, the angle of bank must be increased 
F.Slipping Turns 
i.In a slipping turn, the rate of turn is too slow for the angle of bank, and the plane is yawed to the 
outside of the turning ﬂight path 
a.The horizontal component (HCL) of lib is greater than Centrifugal Force (CF) 
ii.HCL and CF equilibrium is reestablished by decreasing bank/increasing the rate of turn 
a.Increase or decrease rudder pressure to center the ball or adjust bank 
G.Skidding Turns 
i.In a skidding turn, the rate of turn is too great for the angle of bank and the plane is yawed inside 
the turn 
a.There is excess centrifugal force compared to the HCL

12.Stalls

iii.Turning Flight 
a.The stalling speed of an aircrab is higher in a level turn than in straight and level ﬂight

a.The wing must produce suﬃcient addi3onal lib to counteract the load imposed 
b.In a turn, the necessary addi3onal lib is acquired by applying back pressure 
•This increases the wings AOA (AOA increases with the bank angle to maintain level ﬂight) 
c.If at any 3me during a turn the AOA becomes excessive, the airplane will stall

II.E. Airplane Flight Controls 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Learning how the ﬂight controls work and why the inputs you make result in the corresponding changes. This 
is what is actually going on when you move the control surfaces, adjust trim, or use the ﬂaps. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
The airplane’s aptude (rota3on around the 3 axes) is controlled by deﬂec3on of the primary ﬂight controls. 
These are hinged, moveable surfaces amached to the trailing edge of the wings and ver3cal and horizontal 
stabilizers. When deﬂected, these surfaces change the camber and angle of amack of the wing or stabilizer 
and thus change its lib and drag characteris3cs. Trim controls are used to relieve the control pressures and 
ﬂaps create a compromise between a high cruise speed and low landing speed. 
Why 
Understanding how the airplane func3ons and the eﬀects each control input will have on the airplane results 
in an understanding of how to control the airplane. Understanding how the airplane works results in a much 
more proﬁcient pilot. 
How: 
1.Overview 
A.Chord Line – An imaginary straight line drawn through an airfoil from the leading to the trailing edge

II.F. Airplane Weight and Balance 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
The earliest airplanes could barely lib the pilot and enough fuel for a few minutes of ﬂight. Many could not 
get airborne on a warm day. The ﬁrst Wright ﬂyer could only carry the pilot and a few ounces of fuel if the 
headwind was at least 11 mph! Planes have come a long way and pilots s3ll need to balance the plane’s load. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Airplane weight and balance is basically balancing the airplane within approved limits. 
Why 
Compliance with the weight and balance limits is cri3cal to ﬂight safety. Opera3ng above the maximum 
weight limits compromises the structural integrity of the aircrab and aﬀects performance. Opera3on with the 
center of gravity outside the approved limits results in control diﬃculty. 
How: 
1.Terms 
A.Reference Datum (RD) - an imaginary ver3cal plane or line from which all measurements of arm are 
taken 
i.The datum may be located anywhere the manufacturer chooses 
ii.Common loca3ons are the nose, the engine ﬁrewall, the wing’s leading edge, or ahead of the nose 
iii.Once the datum has been selected, all moment arms and the loca3on of CG range are measured 
from this point 
B.Center of Gravity (CG) – the point at which an airplane would balance if it were suspended at that point 
i.The distance of the CG from the RD is found by dividing the total moment by total weight 
C.Arm – the horizontal distance in inches from the reference datum line to the CG of an item 
i.Plus (+) = measured ab of the datum 
ii.Minus (-) = measured forward of the datum 
iii.If the RD is ahead of the nose, all of the arms are posi3ve 
D.Basic Empty Weight – the weight of the standard airplane, op3onal equipment, unusable fuel, and full 
opera3ng ﬂuids (including oil) 
E.CG Limits – the speciﬁed forward and ab points within which the CG must be located during the ﬂight 
F.Maximum Landing Weight – the greatest weight that an aircrab is normally allowed to have at landing 
G.Maximum Ramp Weight – the total permimed weight of a loaded aircrab, including all fuel 
i.It is greater than the takeoﬀ weight due to the fuel that will be burned during taxi and run-up 
ii.Also referred to as taxi weight 
H.Maximum Takeoﬀ Weight – the maximum allowable weight for takeoﬀ 
I.Maximum Zero Fuel Weight – the maximum weight, exclusive of usable fuel 
J.Moment – the product of the weight of an item mul3plied by its arm and expressed in pound-inches 
i.Total moment is the weight of the airplane mul3plied by the distance between the datum and CG 
K.Moment Index – a moment divided by a constant such as 100, 1,000 or 10,000 
i.The purpose is to simplify weight and balance computa3ons 
L.Payload – the weight of the occupants, cargo and baggage 
M.Standard Weights – established weights for numerous items in weight and balance computa3ons

2.Weight and Flight Performance 
A.Weight and Flight Performance 
i.Any added weight reduces aircrab performance 
ii.Manufacturer’s limit maximum weights to ensure aircrab performance / structural abili3es  
a.Verify required performance based on the airplane weight and current condi3ons 
iii.Eﬀects of increased weight 
a.Higher takeoﬀ speed and longer takeoﬀ run  
b.Reduced rate and angle of climb 
c.Lower maximum al3tude 
d.Slower cruise speed and reduced range, and increased fuel consump3on   
e.Reduced maneuverability 
f.Higher stall speed 
g.Higher approach speed and longer landing roll 
h.Excessive weight on the nose / tail wheel 
iv.Eﬀects of Overloading 
a.Degraded climb performance, may not even be able to takeoﬀ 
•Even a minor overload may make it impossible to clear an otherwise normal obstacle  
•May not be able to reach manufacturer’s published maximum al3tudes 
b.Overhea3ng during climbs, added wear on engine parts 
c.Overstressing the aircrab 
B.Weight and Structure 
i.In loading an aircrab, the structure must be considered 
a.Structural failures which result from overloading may be catastrophic but they oben aﬀect 
structure progressively, making it diﬃcult to detect or repair 
b.Airworthiness requirements prescribe that the structure of an aircrab can withstand a speciﬁc 
load factor (3.8 G’s for normal category) 
•This means the primary structure can withstand a load of 3.8 3mes the approved gross 
weight of the aircrab without structural failure occurring 
•Any overload is ampliﬁed in the case the aircrab is stressed to these G limits 
a.For example, a 100 lb. overload imposes a poten3al structural overload of 380 lbs. 
c.Even seats, baggage compartments, and cabin ﬂoors are designed for a certain load 
d.Follow the manufacturer’s guidelines and placards in regards to weight 
ii.Habitual overloading tends to cause cumula3ve stress and damage that may not be detected and 
result in structural failure at a later 3me, during normal opera3ons 
C.Stability and Controllability  
i.An airplane with forward loading  
a.A forward CG/nose-heavy condi3on causes problems controlling and raising the nose, especially 
at slow airspeeds (takeoﬀ and landing) 
•During landing, exceeding the forward CG limit may result in excessive loads on the 
nosewheel, higher stalling speeds and higher control forces 
•In extreme cases, it may be diﬃcult or impossible to ﬂare for landing 
b.The airplane is “heavier” and consequently slower than the same airplane with a further ab CG

II.F. Airplane Weight and Balance 
• Addi3onal back pressure than normally would be required is necessary to maintain al3tude 
•The added back pressure requires the tail surfaces to produce a greater down force  
•The greater down force adds to wing 
loading, increasing the total lib required 
from the wings 
•Thus, the nose heavy aircrab requires a 
higher AOA to maintain al3tude, which 
results in more drag and, in turn, 
produces a higher stalling speed 
c.The airplane is more controllable in a stall 
•The longer arm from the CG makes the 
elevator more eﬀec3ve 
•The nose heavy loading results in a 
tendency for the nose to drop, or assist in 
breaking the stall 
ii.An airplane with ab loading 
a.A tail-heavy condi3on has serious eﬀect upon 
longitudinal stability, and reduces the capability to recover from stalls and spins 
•It also produces very light control forces, another undesirable characteris3c 
a.Very easy to overstress the airplane 
b.The airplane is “lighter” and consequently faster than the same airplane with a more forward CG 
•Less back pressure than normally would be required is necessary to maintain al3tude 
•The reduced back pressure requires less down force from the tail surfaces 
•The reduced down force reduces wing loading, decreasing the total lib required from the 
wings 
•Thus, tail heavy loading requires a lower AOA to maintain al3tude, which results in less drag, 
and in turn, produces a lower stalling speed 
c.Although the stall speed is lower, the airplane less controllable in a stall as the CG moves ab 
•The airplane is less controllable due to the shorter arm from the CG to the elevator 
a.Greater deﬂec3on is required to produce the same result as with a farther forward CG 
•The tail-heavy aircrab also has less of a tendency to pitch down in the case of a stall 
b.There is a point in rearward loading of an aircrab at which a ﬂat spin develops 
1.A ﬂat spin is impossible to get the nose down and recover from 
iii.The CG and Lateral Loading 
a.Unbalanced lateral loading (more weight on the right or leb side of the aircrab centerline) may 
result in adverse eﬀects 
•This can be caused by: fuel imbalance, people, baggage, etc. 
b.Compensate for any imbalance with trim (if available), or constant control pressure 
•This places the aircrab in an out-of-streamline condi3on, increasing drag, and decreasing 
eﬃciency

•If you know 3 of the components, you can solve for the 4th 
b.For example, if the total weight of the aircrab is 8,000 pounds, and you move a 100 pounds of

•                  12,000                                    
   
•In this case, the CG moved 1.5” (add or subtract it from the original CG as appropriate) 
ii.Adding or Removing Weight 
a.Formula:  
  
•Just like above, solve for the missing component  
b.For example, if the airplane weighs 6,100 pounds, with a CG at 80” , where does the CG end up if 
100 pounds is removed from sta3on 150? 
•            7,000                        
   
•If the CG is shibing ab, the  is added to the old CG 
•If the CG is shibing forward, the  is subtracted from the old CG 
•In this case, the CG moved 1.2” forward, and the new CG = 78.8”  (80 – 1.2)

What 
Naviga3on and ﬂight planning is the process of planning and execu3ng cross country ﬂights.

1.Terms 
A.Naviga3on Terminology 
i.True North – Points directly to the geographic north pol 
ii.Magne3c North – Aligns with Earth’s magne3c ﬁeld and points directly to the magne3c north pole 
iii.Varia3on – The angular diﬀerence between true north and magne3c north; isogonic lines on charts 
iv.True Course – The direc3on of ﬂight as measured on a chart clockwise from true North 
v.True Heading – The direc3on the longitudinal axis of the airplane points with respect to true North 
a.True heading equals true course plus or minus any wind correc3on angle 
vi.Magne3c Course – True course corrected for magne3c varia3on 
vii.Magne3c Heading – Magne3c Course corrected for wind (direc3on and speed) 
viii.Compass Heading – Aircrab heading read from the compass 
a.Derived by applying correc3on factors for varia3on, devia3on, and wind to your true course 
ix.Devia3on – Compass error due to magne3c disturbances from electrical/metal parts in the plane 
a.The correc3on for this is displayed on a compass correc3on card near the magne3c compass 
B.Atmospheric Terminology  
i.Standard Pressure – 29.92” Hg (at sea level) 
ii.Standard Temperature – 15o C / 59oF (at sea level) 
C.Al3tude Terminology 
i.Indicated Alt –Al3tude read directly from the al3meter aber it’s set to the current al3meter sepng 
ii.Pressure Alt – Height above the standard pressure level of 29.92 in Hg - 
 
a.Obtained by sepng 29.92 in the barometric pressure window and reading the al3meter 
iii.Density Alt – Pressure al3tude corrected for nonstandard temperatures -  
a.The equa3on above is not exact 
b.Directly related to an aircrab’s takeoﬀ, climb, and landing performance 
iv.True Al3tude – The true ver3cal distance of the aircrab above sea level 
a.Airport, terrain, and obstacle eleva3ons found on aeronau3cal charts are true al3tudes

II.H. Night Opera3ons 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
A lot of people prefer night ﬂying to day ﬂying.  The air tends to be smoother, the radios tend to be quieter, 
there’s less traﬃc, and it’s more relaxing. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Night opera3ons are the factors dealing with the opera3on of the airplane at night. 
Why 
Night ﬂying is very diﬀerent from day ﬂying - The eyes func3on diﬀerently at night, references available in the 
day are no longer available at night, there are many illusions that can aﬀect a pilot at night, and more. Flying 
at night presents unique situa3ons which, if ignored, can lead to dangerous situa3ons.  
How:  
1.Eyes at Night 
A.Rods and Cones 
i.Light enters the eye through the cornea, travels through the lens, and falls on the re3na 
ii.The re3na contains light sensi3ve cells that convert light into electrical impulses which are sent to 
the brain 
a.There are two types of light-sensi3ve cells, Rods and Cones: 
•Cones - Responsible for color, detail, and far away objects 
a.The cones are located in the center of the re3na 
•Rods – Func3on when something is seen in the peripherals and provide vision in dim light 
b.The rods are located in a ring around the cones (peripherals) 
iii.The rods and cones are used diﬀerently depending on the ambient light condi3ons

II.H. Night Opera3ons 
a.Types of vision: Photopic, Mesopic, Scotopic 
b.Both the cones and rods are used for vision in the day 
•But, without normal light, the process of night vision is placed almost en3rely on the rods 
iv.Rods, Cones, and Night Vision 
a.Cones are located in the center of the re3na (the layer upon which all images are focused) 
•There is a small pit called the fovea where almost all the light sensing cells are cones 
a.This is the area where most looking occurs (your center of vision) 
b.The Rods 
•Make night vision possible 
•During daylight, objects can be seen by looking 
directly at them, using the fovea, but at night a 
scanning procedure to permit oﬀ center 
viewing is more eﬀec3ve 
1.The cones need light to func3on, 
without suﬃcient light (at night, for 
example) the cones are eﬀec3vely a 
blind spot 
•Rods are concentrated around the cones and 
are used to see in dim light 
b.Since cones are only useful with suﬃcient 
light and the rods lie outside the fovea 
(outside the center of vision), oﬀ-center 
viewing is used for night ﬂight 
c.When amemp3ng to ﬁnd traﬃc do not 
stare directly at it, look slightly oﬀ to the 
leb or right to allow the rods to see the 
aircrab  
•The problem with rods is that a large amount 
of light overwhelms them and they take a long 
3me to reset and adapt to the dark again (Ex: 
stepping out of a dark movie theatre into the 
daylight) 
d.The rods can take approximately 30 
minutes to fully adapt to the dark 
1.Once fully adapted, the Rods are 
about 10,000x more sensi3ve to light 
e.Aber the rods have adapted to the dark, the process is reversed when exposed to light 
1.The eyes adjust to the light in a mamer of seconds 
2.If a dark room is reentered, the 30-min process to adapt is started again 
a.Therefore, it is important to avoid bright lights before and during a ﬂight 
i.This is why red ﬂashlights are recommended during ﬂight, they do not 
disrupt the rods dark adapta3on

II.H. Night Opera3ons 
v.Summary 
a.Night vision is based on the rods and oﬀ-center viewing is necessary 
b.Staring directly at an object at night could result in not seeing the object at all since the cones in 
the center of your vision are considerably less eﬀec3ve without suﬃcient light

2.Disorienta8on and Night Op8cal Illusions 
A.In addi3on to night vision limita3ons, night vision illusions can cause confusion 
B.Combapng Disorienta3on / Illusions  
i.Verify Aptude by Reference to the Flight Instruments 
a.Reference to the ﬂight instruments is the best way to cope with disorienta3on/op3cal illusions 
ii.Use ver3cal guidance as much as possible, especially at night

iv.If at any 3me the pilot is unsure of their posi3on, a go around should be executed 
C.Autokinesis 
i.Caused by staring at a single point of light against a dark background for over a few seconds 
ii.The light appears to move on its own 
iii.Prevent this by focusing the eyes on objects at varying distances and avoid ﬁxa3ng 
a.Keep the eyes moving and oﬀset/use peripherals 
D.Reversible Perspec3ve Illusion 
i.At night, an aircrab may appear to be moving away from a second aircrab when it is, in fact, 
approaching the second aircrab 
ii.Oben occurs when ﬂying parallel to another’s course 
iii.Observe the aircrab lights and their posi3on on the horizon 
a.If the light intensity increases, the aircrab is approaching 
b.If they dim, it is moving away 
E.Size-Distance Illusion 
i.When viewing a source of light that is gepng brighter or dimmer, pilots may instead interpret it as 
approaching or retrea3ng 
F.Flicker Ver3go 
i.A light ﬂickering between 4 and 20 cycles per second can produce unpleasant, dangerous reac3ons 
a.Examples: nausea, vomi3ng, and ver3go. Convulsions/unconsciousness are possible but rare 
ii.Proper scanning techniques at night can prevent pilots from ﬂicker ver3go 
G.Featureless Terrain 
i.An absence of ground features can create the illusion that the aircrab is higher than it actually is 
ii.This results in a tendency to ﬂy a lower-than-normal approach 
a.Elements that can cause visual obscurity can do the same (rain, haze, dark runway environment) 
H.Ground Ligh3ng 
i.Regularly spaced lights along a road/highway/etc. can appear to be runway lights 
ii.Lights on moving trains have been mistaken for runway/approach lights 
iii.Bright runway or approach lights can create the illusion the airplane is closer to the runway  
iv.Mi3gate this as much as possible by maintaining situa3onal awareness  
a.Know what to expect to see (type of airport/runway ligh3ng), where you expect to see it and 
know where you are (use navaids, GPS, landmarks, etc.) 
I.False Horizon 
i.Caused when the natural horizon is obscured/not readily apparent 
a.Generated by confusing bright stars and city lights

Acen8on

So, you want to ﬂy really high? It’s not just that simple. A lot changes as the al3tude increases. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
The required equipment, how it func3ons, the unique hazards and regula3ons associated with ﬂying at high 
al3tudes. 
Why 
There are many advantages to ﬂying at high al3tudes (jet engines are more eﬃcient, weather and turbulence 
can be avoided, etc.). Many modern GA airplanes are being designed to operate in the high al3tude 
environment, therefore it is important that pilots be familiar with at least the basic opera3ng principles. 
How: 
1.The High-Al8tude Flight Environment 
A.FAR 61.31(g) considers all ﬂight opera3ons conducted above 25,000’ MSL to be high al3tude, however 
many eﬀects of higher al3tudes can be felt well below 25,000’ 
2.Regulatory Requirements (FAR 91.211) 
A.No person may operate a civil aircrab of US registry at cabin pressure al3tudes above: 
i.12,500’ MSL up to/including 14,000’ unless the required minimum ﬂight crew is provided with and 
uses supplemental oxygen for the part of the ﬂight at those al3tudes over 30 minutes 
ii.14,000’ unless the required min ﬂight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen during 
the en3re ﬂight 3me at those al3tudes 
iii.15,000’ unless each occupant of the aircrab is provided with supplemental oxygen 
B.No person may operate a civil aircrab of US registry with a pressurized cabin at ﬂight al3tudes above: 
i.FL 250 unless at least a 10-minute supply of supplemental oxygen, in addi3on to any oxygen required 
to sa3sfy the paragraph above, is available for each occupant of the aircrab for use in the event that 
a descent is necessitated by a loss of cabin pressure 
ii.FL 350, unless one pilot at the controls of the airplane is wearing and using an oxygen mask that is 
secured and sealed (and that either supplies oxygen at all 3mes or automa3cally whenever the cabin 
pressure exceeds 14,000’ MSL) 
a.Excep3on: One pilot need not wear and use an oxygen mask while at or below FL 410 if there are 
two pilots at the controls and each pilot has a quick donning type of oxygen mask that can be 
placed on the face with one hand from the ready posi3on within 5 seconds, supplying oxygen 
and properly secured and sealed 
b.Above FL 350: If for any reason at any 3me, one pilot leaves the controls the remaining pilot shall 
put on and use an oxygen mask un3l the other pilot has returned  
3.Physiological Hazards 
A.The human body func3ons normally from sea level to 12,000’ MSL 
i.Brain oxygen satura3on is at a level for normal func3on (Op3mal func3oning is 96% satura3on) 
a.At 12,000’ , oxygen satura3on is approx. 87%, which gets close to a performance aﬀec3ng level 
b.Above 12,000’ oxygen satura3on con3nues to decrease and aﬀect performance

E.Trapped Gas 
i.Gases expand with any decrease in pressure – if you reduce the pressure, as you ascend to al3tude, 
gases increase in volume, and then decrease in volume during descent 
ii.The body has several cavi3es that contain varying amounts of gas 
a.Most cavi3es can allow the gas to escape, but if the gas gets trapped it can result in pain 
b.Problem areas include: middle ear, sinuses, teeth, and GI tract 
F.Nitrogen Absorp3on (Decompression Sickness - DCS) 
i.One of the more dangerous problems  
a.At sea level, the nitrogen inside the body and outside the body is in equilibrium 
b.When atmospheric pressure is reduced, the equilibrium is upset and nitrogen leaves the body 
c.If the nitrogen leaves too quickly, bubbles may form causing a variety of symptoms 
ii.Evolving and expanding gases in the body are known as decompression sickness. There are 2 groups: 
a.Trapped Gas: expanding or contrac3ng gas in certain body cavi3es during al3tude changes can 
result in abdominal pain, toothache, or pain in ears and sinuses if the person is unable to 
equalize the pressure changes 
b.Evolved Gas: When the pressure on the body drops suﬃciently, nitrogen comes out of solu3on 
and forms bubbles which can have adverse eﬀects on some body 3ssues

4.Pressuriza8on in Airplanes

iii.Air is released from the fuselage through an 
ouqlow valve 
a.By regula3ng the air exi3ng the airplane, the

to the pressurized area

b.When the aircrab reaches the

•The ﬂow of compressed air is regulated by an ouqlow valve which keeps pressure at the

7.Care and Storage of High-Pressure Oxygen Bocles 
A.If the airplane does not have a ﬁxed installa3on, portable oxygen equipment must be accessible in ﬂight 
B.Oxygen is usually stored in high pressure containers at 1,800 – 2,200 psi 
i.When the ambient temperature surrounding the cylinder decreases, pressure within will decrease 
a.This occurs because pressure varies directly with temperature if the volume of a gas remains 
constant 
b.A drop in the indicated pressure may be due to the container being stored in an unheated area 
of the aircrab, rather than deple3on of the oxygen supply 
ii.High pressure containers should be marked with the psi tolerance before ﬁlling to that pressure 
a.The oxygen used should meet or exceed SAE AS8010, Avia3on Breathing Oxygen Purity Standard 
C.Be aware of the danger of ﬁre when using oxygen 
i.Materials that are nearly ﬁre proof in ordinary air may be suscep3ble to combus3on in oxygen 
a.Oils and greases may catch ﬁre if exposed to pure oxygen and cannot be used in oxygen systems

D.Before each ﬂight, thoroughly inspect and test all oxygen equipment 
i.Examine the equipment - available supply, opera3onal check, and assure it is readily available

8.Rapid Decompression Problems and their Solu8ons 
A.Decompression is the inability of the pressuriza3on system to maintain its designed pressure diﬀeren3al 
i.This can be caused by a malfunc3on in the pressuriza3on system or structural damage to the plane 
a.If the turbo charger fails, not only will the airplane descend, but pressuriza3on will be lost 
B.Two categories of decompression 
i.Explosive Decompression – A change in cabin pressure faster than the lungs can decompress (< 0.5 
seconds. Possibly leading to lung damage) 
ii.Rapid Decompression – A change in cabin pressure where the lungs can decompress faster than the 
cabin (therefore there is no likelihood of lung damage) 
C.Indica3ons of a Rapid or Explosive Decompression 
i.During explosive decompression, there may be noise and one may feel dazed for a second 
ii.During most decompressions, the cabin will ﬁll with fog, dust, ﬂying debris 
a.Fog is the result of the rapid change in temperature and change of rela3ve humidity 
iii.Air will rush from the mouth and nose due to the escape of air from the lungs 
D.The primary danger of decompression is hypoxia 
i.Quick, proper u3liza3on of oxygen equipment is necessary to avoid unconsciousness 
ii.Another poten3al danger is decompression sickness, as discussed above 
E.Supplemental oxygen and a rapid descent from al3tude is necessary in order to minimize the problems 
associated with decompression 
Conclusion: 
Brief review of the main points 
The fundamental concept of cabin pressuriza3on is that it is the compression of air in the airplane’s cabin to 
maintain a cabin al3tude lower than the actual ﬂight al3tude. If your airplane is equipped with a pressuriza3on 
system, you must know the normal and emergency opera3ng procedures.

II.K. Na3onal Airspace System 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Each type of airspace is like a diﬀerent country. Each type of airspace has its own controllers or rulers, its own 
rules for those in their ‘territory,’ and its own beneﬁts or services which are provided to those within its 
borders. Borders are drawn and there are requirements and permission necessary to enter certain airspaces 
(e.g. Passport).  
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What:   
Airspace is deﬁned as, “the por3on of the atmosphere above a par3cular land area, especially above a 
na3on.” The atmosphere above the United States is divided into several sectors, or classes and in each 
diﬀerent airspace class, speciﬁc rules apply. 
Why:  
Diﬀerent airspaces have been deﬁned to eﬃciently manage the large amount of air traﬃc that traverses the 
sky each day.  In order to ﬂy from place to place a pilot must know the rules and requirements regarding 
airspace.

2.Special VFR (FAR 91.157) 
A.Clearance to operate under VFR with less than VFR weather minimums 
i.Only in Class B, C, D, or E surface areas, below 10,000’ MSL 
ii.Must be requested by the pilot 
iii.Special VFR is on the basis of weather condi3ons at the airport of intended landing/departure  
iv.Only approved if IFR traﬃc are not delayed  
B.Special VFR may only be conducted 
i.With an ATC clearance 
ii.Clear of clouds 
iii.With at least 1 statute mile ﬂight visibility 
iv.At night (sunset to sunrise): 
a.With an instrument rated pilot and aircrab 
C.May not takeoﬀ or land under special VFR unless ground visibility is at least 1 statute mile 
i.If not reported, ﬂight visibility must be at least 1 statute mile 
a.Flight visibility includes the visibility from the cockpit of an aircrab in takeoﬀ posi3on, if: 
•Flight is conducted under Part 91, and 
•The airport is a satellite airport without weather repor3ng capabili3es  
D.Special VFR is prohibited at certain airports (mostly large class B airports) shown in Part 91 Appendix D 
Sec3on 3 
3.Special Use Airspace 
Special Use airspace exists where ac3vi3es must be conﬁned because of their nature.  In special use 
airspace, limita3ons may be placed on aircrab that are not a part of the ac3vi3es. 
A.Prohibited Areas 
i.Airspace within which the ﬂight of aircrab is prohibited 
ii.Established for security or other reasons associated with the na3onal welfare 
iii.Published in the Federal Register and are depicted on aeronau3cal charts 
B.Restricted Areas 
i.Areas where opera3ons are hazardous to nonpar3cipa3ng aircrab and contain airspace within which 
the ﬂight of aircrab, while not wholly prohibited, is subject to restric3ons 
ii.Can contain unusual, oben invisible hazards to aircrab (e.g. ar3llery ﬁring, aerial gunnery, or guided 
missiles) 
iii.Penetra3on without authoriza3on from the using or controlling agency may be extremely hazardous 
a.IFR ﬂights may be authorized to transit the airspace and are routed accordingly 
iv.Restricted areas are depicted on aeronau3cal charts and are published in the Federal Register 
C.Warning Areas 
i.Airspace of deﬁned dimensions, extending from 3 nm outward from the coast of the US, containing 
ac3vity that may be hazardous to nonpar3cipa3ng aircrab 
a.The ac3vi3es may be much the same as those for a restricted area 
ii.The purpose is to warn nonpar3cipa3ng pilots of the poten3al danger 
iii.They are depicted on aeronau3cal charts 
D.MOAs (Military Opera3on Areas) 
i.Consist of airspace with deﬁned ver3cal and lateral limits established for the purpose of separa3ng 
certain military training ac3vity from IFR traﬃc 
ii.IFR traﬃc may be cleared through a MOA if ATC can maintain IFR separa3on, otherwise expect a 
reroute  
iii.There is no restric3on against a pilot opera3ng VFR in these areas 
a.A pilot should, although, be alert since training ac3vi3es may include aeroba3c and abrupt 
maneuvers 
iv.MOAs are depicted on aeronau3cal charts

1.VOR / VORTAC (Very High Frequency Omnidirec3onal Range) 
i.What is it? 
a.Omni means all 
•An omnidirec3onal range is a VHF radio transmipng ground sta3on that projects straight 
line courses (or radials) from the sta3on in all direc3ons 
a.It can be visualized from the top as being similar to the spokes from the hub of a wheel 
b.The radials projected are referenced to magne3c north 
•A radial is deﬁned as a line of magne3c bearing extending outward from the VOR sta3on 
•The accuracy of course alignment with radials is considered to be excellent (± 1o) 
VOR ground sta3ons transmit within a VHF frequency band of 108.0 – 117.95 MHz 
•Because the equipment is VHF , the signals are subject to line-of-sight restric3ons 
a.Range varies in propor3on to al3tude  
c.The distance the radials are projected depends on the power of the transmimer 
d.VORs are classed according to opera3onal use in 3 classes with varying normal useful ranges: 
•T (Terminal); L (Low Alt); H (High Alt) 
ii.Three types of VORS 
a.VOR – The VOR by itself. Provides magne3c bearing informa3on to and from the sta3on 
b.VOR/DME –DME (Distance Measuring Equipment) is installed with the VOR (more info below) 
c.VORTAC – Military tac3cal air naviga3ons (TACAN) equipment is installed with a VOR

B.GPS 
i.The GPS system is composed of 3 major elements 
a.The Space Segment 
•Composed of a constella3on of 31 satellites approximately 11,000 NM above the earth 
a.The US is commimed to maintain 24 opera3onal satellites 95% of the 3me

•Consists of all components associated with the GPS receiver 
a.Range from portable, hand-held receivers to those permanently installed in the plane

b.Posi3oning, velocity, and precise 3ming to the user

C.WAAS (basically augmented GPS, to the point it may be used for precision approaches) 
i.Designed to improve the accuracy, integrity, and availability of GPS signals 
a.Integrity is improved through real-3me monitoring of the satellites  
•Has the ability to provide 3mely warnings when the signal is providing misleading data that 
could be poten3ally hazardous 
•WAAS cer3ﬁca3on required proving there is only an extremely small probability that an 
error would go undetected – equivalent of no more than 3 seconds of bad data per year  
b.Accuracy is improved by providing correc3ons to the satellites to reduce errors 
•A network of ground-based sta3ons measure small varia3ons in satellite signals  
•Measurements are routed to a master sta3on 
•The master sta3on sends the correc3on messages to the satellites which broadcast the 
message, allowing WAAS enabled receivers to compute a more accurate posi3on 
c.As a result, performance improvement is suﬃcient to enable approach procedures with GPS/
WAAS glidepaths  
•WAAS requires a posi3on accuracy of 25’ or less at least 95% of the 3me 
a.Actual performance measurements have shown it typically provides bemer than 1 meter 
laterally, and 1.5 meters ver3cally 
•WAAS is capable of achieving the required Category 1 precision approach accuracy of 16 
meters laterally and 4 meters ver3cally

b.Can be further enhanced with LAAS

ii.All-weather aircrab landing system based on real-3me diﬀeren3al correc3on of the GPS signal.  
iii.Local reference receivers located around the airport send data to a central loca3on at the airport 
a.This data is used to formulate a correc3on message, which is then transmimed to users via a VHF

iv.A receiver on an aircrab uses this informa3on to correct GPS signals, which then provides a

6.ADS-B (Automa8c Dependent Surveillance – Broadcast) Basics 
A.What is it? 
i.Founda3on for NextGen moving from ground radar to satellites  
a.More precise tracking: Broadcasts every second vs a radar sweep every 5-12 seconds 
b.Radar waves are limited to line-of-sight and installa3on sites 
•ADS-B combines ground sta3ons/satellites for bemer visibility regardless of terrain/obstacles  
•ADS-B ground sta3ons are much easier to install than radars 
ii.ADS-B 
a.Automa3c: Automa3cally transmits informa3on 
b.Dependent: Posi3on/velocity are derived from GPS/FMS 
c.Surveillance: Allows 3D posi3on and iden3ﬁca3on  
d.Broadcast: Transmits the informa3on to anyone with appropriate receiving equipment 
iii.ADS-B Out

iv.ADS-B In

•Provides weather and traﬃc posi3on informa3on directly to the cockpit 
a.Graphical weather displays, advisories (NOTAMs, weather, terrain, TFRs, etc.) 
b.FIS-B (Flight Informa3on Service Broadcast – available on 978 MHz UAT equipment) 
•Similar to XM weather, but more informa3on

c.TIS-B (Traﬃc Informa3on Service Broadcast – available to 1090ES and UAT equipment users) 
•Provides traﬃc informa3on on all transponder-based aircrab in the vicinity of the ADS-B

•At and above 3,000’ MSL over the Gulf of Mexico within 12 nm of the coast

iii.ADS-B Devia3on Authoriza3on

•Must be equipped with opera3onal transponder and al3tude encoder

When naviga3ng with a VOR and you wish to head toward the sta3on ensure the ﬂag indicates “TO” and follow 
the indicated heading. When it is necessary to track away from the sta3on, ensure the ﬂag indicates “FROM” and 
follow the heading indicated.  Failing to do this could result in reverse sensing (not applicable to an HSI). GPS is a 
satellite-based system that used for naviga3on. WAAS and LAAS are also satellite based naviga3on systems but 
they augment the GPS system with ground-based sta3ons allowing for more precise loca3on informa3on as well 
as ver3cal guidance. The radar services provided by ATC can be very helpful in almost any ﬂight.

Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Instead of gepng ourselves stuck, in the air, in a thunderstorm or some sort of extreme weather we should 
have a good understanding of weather informa3on in order to know when to and not to ﬂy.  
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Through a complex system of weather services, government agencies, and independent weather observers, 
pilots are given vast informa3on regarding weather pamerns, trends, and characteris3cs in the form of up-to-
date weather reports and forecasts 
Why 
These reports and forecasts enable pilots to make informed decisions regarding weather and ﬂight safety. 
How: 
1.Importance of a Thorough Weather Brieﬁng 
A.FAR 91.103 – As PIC, you are required to become familiar with the weather reports and forecasts 
B.The weather brieﬁng allows the pilot to make a more educated and competent go/no go decision 
i.Alerts the pilot to any poten3ally hazardous condi3ons along the route of ﬂight while providing a big 
picture overview of the condi3ons prior to stepping foot in the airplane 
ii.More speciﬁc informa3on is also amained 
iii.The weather brieﬁng can go beyond just weather, providing the pilot informa3on on NOTAMs, ATC 
delays, and other informa3on that may aﬀect the ﬂight 
C.The pilot knows what to expect and can be alert to any changing condi3ons while enroute 
2.Weather Informa8on Sources 
A.General awareness of the overall weather 
i.Internet, Weather Apps, TV, etc. 
B.Detailed Brieﬁng (Speciﬁc to the ﬂight) 
i.FSS (1-800-WX BRIEF or 1800wxbrief.com) 
a.Primary source for preﬂight weather 
b.Provides NOTAM, weather, and ﬁling of ﬂight plans 
ii.NWS – Na3onal Weather Service 
a.Avia3onweather .gov 
b.Provides weather only (vs FSS with NOTAM, and ﬁling of ﬂight plans) 
iii.ForeFlight 
a.Brieﬁngs are 3mestamped and stored to comply with FAR 91.103  
iv.AIM 7-1-2-C  
a.Pilots can receive a regulatory compliant brieﬁng without contac3ng ﬂight service 
b.Encouraged to use automated resources & review AC 91-92 – Pilot’s Guide to a Preﬂight Brieﬁng 
•Provides a roadmap for self-brieﬁngs and guidance for FAR 91.103 required preﬂight ac3ons 
•Brieﬁng types and sources, sample preﬂight checklists, Do’s and Don’ts, and more

i.FSS Frequencies 
a.Provides informa3on/services before, during, and aber ﬂights,

C.Wind Shear 
i.What is it? 
a.A sudden, dras3c change in wind speed and/or direc3on over a very small area 
b.While wind shear can occur at any al3tude, low-level wind shear is especially hazardous due to 
the proximity to the ground 
•Low-level wind shear is commonly associated with passing frontal systems, thunderstorms, 
temperature inversions, and strong upper-level winds (greater than 25 knots) 
ii.Why is it dangerous? 
a.Wind shear can subject an aircrab to violent updrabs and downdrabs, as well as abrupt changes 
to the horizontal movement of the aircrab 
b.It can rapidly change the performance of the aircrab and disrupt the normal ﬂight aptude, for 
example: 
•A tailwind can quickly change to a headwind causing an increase in airspeed and 
performance  
•A headwind can quickly change to a tailwind causing a decrease in airspeed and 
performance 
c.Microbursts 
•The most severe type of wind shear 
a.Associated with convec3ve precipita3on into dry air at cloud base 
•Typical Microburst 
b.Horizontal diameter of 1-2 miles 
c.Depth of 1,000’ 
d.Lifespan of 5-15 minutes 
e.Downdrabs of up to 6,000 feet per minute 
f.Headwind losses of 30-90 knots (seriously degraded performance) 
g.Strong turbulence and hazardous wind direc3on changes 
•Flying through a Microburst 
h.During an inadvertent takeoﬀ into a microburst, the plane may ﬁrst experience a 
performance-increasing headwind (1) 
i.Followed by performance-decreasing downdrabs (2) 
j.Followed by a rapidly increasing tailwind (3) 
1.This can result in terrain impact or ﬂight dangerously close to the ground (4) 
k.An encounter during approach involves the same sequence of wind changes and could 
force the plane to the ground short of the runway

a.A dangerous convec3ve storm that consists of primarily a single, quasi-steady rota3ng updrab

9.Frost & Icing 
A.Frost 
i.On cool, clear nights, the temperature of the ground and objects on the surface can cause 
temperatures of the surrounding air to drop below the dew point. When this occurs, the moisture in 
the air condenses and deposits itself on the ground, buildings, and other objects like aircrab 
a.The moisture is dew. If the temperature is below freezing, the moisture is deposited in the form

b.While dew poses no threat to aircrab, frost poses a deﬁnite ﬂight safety hazard

lib. It also increases drag, which when combined with lowered lib produc3on, can adversely

B.Types of Icing 
i.Structural Icing 
a.Rime Icing  
•Rough, milky, and opaque ice formed by the instantaneous freezing of small, super cooled

•Rime icing forma3on favors colder temperatures, lower liquid water content and small

b.Clear Icing 
•A glossy, clear, or translucent ice formed by rela3vely slow freezing of large, super cooled

•Clear icing condi3ons exist more oben in an environment with warmer temperatures, higher

•Clear ice forms when only a small por3on of the drop freezes immediately while the 
remaining unfrozen por3on ﬂows or smears over the aircrab surface and gradually freezes 
•Clear ice is more hazardous than rime ice

i.Structural icing degrades engine performance

10.Fog 
A.A visible aggregate of minute water droplets that are based at the surface and reduce visibility to less

are above the surface 
B.Types of Fog

a.Produced over a land area when radia3onal cooling reduces the air temperature below its dew

b.Factors favoring forma3on: Shallow surface layer of rela3vely moist air beneath a dry layer, Clear 
skies, and Light surface winds 
•Radia3on fog is restricted to land because water surfaces cool limle from nighpme radia3on. 
It is shallow when wind is calm. Winds up to about 5 knots mix the air slightly and tend to 
deepen the fog by spreading the cooling through a deeper layer . Stronger winds disperse the 
fog or mix the air through a s3ll deeper layer with stratus clouds forming at the top of the 
mixing layer . 
c.Ground fog usually burns oﬀ rapidly aber sunrise. Other radia3on fog generally clears before 
noon (unless clouds move in over the fog) 
ii.Advec3on Fog 
a.Forms when moist air moves over a colder surface, and the subsequent cooling of that air to 
below its dew point. Most common along coastal areas, but oben moves deep in con3nental 
areas. Advec3on fog deepens as wind speed increases up to 15 knots; winds much stronger than 
15 knots libs the fog into a layer of low stratus or stratocumulus clouds. 
•West coast of the US is quite vulnerable to advec3on fog which frequently forms oﬀshore as

C.Adjustable Pitch (Constant-speed propeller)

ii.How it Works 
a.Once a speciﬁc rpm is selected, the governor automa3cally adjusts the propeller blade to 
maintain the selected rpm 
•For example, aber sepng the rpm, an increase in airspeed or decrease in propeller load 
causes the governor to increase the propeller blade angle to maintain the selected rpm 
a.In this case, the propeller would normally accelerate, but the governor increases the 
blade angle (bigger bites of air) to maintain the desired rpm 
•A reduc3on in airspeed or increase in load causes the propeller blade to decrease 
b.This would slow down a ﬁxed pitch propeller, but the governor decreases the blade 
angle (smaller bites of air) to maintain the same rpm 
b.As long as the propeller blade angle is within its rpm range, a constant rpm is maintained 
•If the propeller blade reaches a pitch stop (i.e. the blade cannot rotate any farther higher or 
lower), the engine rpm will then increase or decrease (like a ﬁxed pitch propeller) 
a.For example, if airspeed decreases enough to rotate the propeller blades un3l they 
contact the low pitch stop, any further decrease in airspeed will cause the engine rpm to 
decrease. The same concept applies to the high pitch stop, but will result in an rpm 
increase

c.Because they are easier to move, to be cer3ﬁed an aircrab must show an increasing resistance to

trailing edge to reduce the control system forces 
b.The stabilator provides extra stability and controllability with less size, drag and weight than 
conven3onal tail surfaces

Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
The inner workings of the airplane; to develop a bemer understanding of what is what, and what is where. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
The main systems found on the Piper Arrow. This includes the primary ﬂight controls and trim, ﬂaps, 
powerplant, propeller, landing gear, fuel, oil and hydraulic systems, electrical and avionics systems, ﬂight 
instruments and the environmental system. 
Why  
Understanding how the airplane works internally will allow for bemer troubleshoo3ng and problem 
iden3ﬁca3on.  The pilot will have a bemer understanding of the airplane as a whole. 
How: 
1.Primary Flight Controls and Trim 
A.Ailerons, Horizontal Tail, and Rudder 
i. General 
a.The basic airframe is of aluminum alloy construc3on 
b.The extremi3es – wing 3ps, cowling, tail surfaces – are of ﬁberglass or ABS thermoplas3c 
c.Cable systems are used between the controls and control surfaces 
ii.Horizontal Tail (Stabilator) 
a.What is a Stabilator? 
•Stabilator – “All-moving tail.” A fully movable aircrab stabilizer 
•A stabilator can allow the pilot to generate a given pitching moment with lower control force 
•Because they are easier to move, to be cer3ﬁed an aircrab must show an increasing 
resistance to increasing pilot input. To provide this resistance, stabilators on small aircrab 
contain an an3-servo trim tab that deﬂects in the same direc3on as the stabilator, providing 
an aerodynamic force resis3ng the pilot’s input   
b.From the POH:  
•The horizontal tail, stabilator, is of the all-movable slab type with a trim tab mounted on the 
trailing edge to reduce the control system forces 
•The stabilator provides extra stability and controllability with less size, drag and weight than 
conven3onal tail surfaces 
iii.Rudder 
a.Conven3onal rudder with rudder trim 
B.Trim 
i.Elevator Trim 
a.As men3oned above, the trim tab is mounted on the trailing edge of the stabilator 
b.The trim tab is actuated by a control wheel on the ﬂoor, between the seats

a.Permits direc3onal trim as needed in ﬂight

III.D. Performance and Limita3ons 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
How exci3ng would it be to ﬁnd out ﬁrst hand, that the airplane actually doesn’t have the ability to takeoﬀ 
from a certain runway and that it also doesn’t have the ability to clear the obstacle at the departure end? 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
The Performance and Limita3ons sec3on of the POH contains the opera3ng data for the airplane; that is, the 
data pertaining to takeoﬀ, climb, range, endurance, descent, and landing. 
Why 
The use of the opera3ng data for the airplane is mandatory for safe and eﬃcient opera3ons 
How: 
1.Determining Weight and Balance 
A.CG = Total Moment divided by Total Weight 
i.Begin with the empty weight and make a list of everything that will be loaded in the airplane 
a.People, items, fuel, etc. (note the weights of everything as well) 
b.Be sure the weight of what you want to load is within the maximum weight limits 
•If the total weight is too high, remove items/people to get within weight limits 
ii.Calculate the Moments of each item 
a.To ﬁnd the moments, use the graph or mul3ply the weight by the arm with the informa3on in 
the POH 
•The weight/moment of the airplane are found in the weight and balance documents 
iii.Then calculate the CG – (Total Moment/Total Weight) 
a.*For the DA20, compare the Total Weight and Total Moment on the graph in supplement 4 
iv.Use the chart in Supplement 4 to determine whether the airplane is within limits 
2.Atmospheric Condi8ons and Performance 
A.Atmospheric Pressure 
i.Though air is light, it has mass and is aﬀected by gravity and therefore it has a force 
ii.Under standard condi3ons at sea level, the average pressure exerted is approx. 14.7 lbs. per sq. in 
iii.Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded 
iv.Density of the air has signiﬁcant eﬀects on the airplane’s performance 
a.As the density of the air increases, airplane performance increases and vice versa 
B.What Changes Air Density (DA)? 
i.Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Al3tude, and Humidity all aﬀect air density 
a.Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases and vice versa 
b.Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases and vice versa 
c.Density varies inversely with al3tude - As al3tude increases, density decreases and vice versa 
d.Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases and vice versa 
•More speciﬁcally: For a given volume of atmospheric air, as humidity increases some of the 
dry air is replaced by water vapor 
a.The molecular weight of dry air is approximately 29 grams/mol, while the molecular 
weight of water vapor (H20) is about 18 grams/mol

1.Grams/mol = Molar mass 
b.As the propor3on of water in the atmosphere (humidity) increases, the density (weight /

C.How it aﬀects Performance 
i.As the air becomes less dense, it reduces: 
a.Power, since the engine takes in less air  
b.Thrust, since the propeller is less eﬃcient in thin air (less air is being moved for every rota3on) 
c.Lib, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils 
D.High al3tude, high temperature airports may not allow safe opera3on 
i.Always be aware of the density al3tude and accompanying performance when planning a ﬂight 
ii.If necessary, delay un3l the performance is amainable, or reduce weight to amain the performance 
3.Performance Charts 
A.Airplane performance is found in Sec3on 5 of the POH (Performance and Limita3ons) 
i.*Supplement 4, for the DA20 (any charts not shown in the supplement are found in Chapter 5) 
B.Using the performance charts, and the accompanying instruc3ons, we can calculate  
i.Cruise Performance 
ii.Stall Speeds based on airplane conﬁgura3on 
iii.Wind Components (Crosswind and Headwind) 
iv.Takeoﬀ Distance and Landing Distance 
v.Climb Performance (In cruise and takeoﬀ conﬁgura3ons as well as Balked Landing) 
vi.True Airspeed 
vii.Maximum Flight Dura3on (Chart in which the Pressure Al3tude is combined with RPM to ﬁnd % bhp, 
KTAS, GPH) 
C.In order to make use of these charts we need to know the Pressure Al3tude (PA) 
i.Pressure Al3tude (PA) – The al3tude indicated when the al3meter sepng window is set to 29.92 
a.PA = 1,000(29.92-Current Al3meter Sepng) + Eleva3on 
•EX: Al3meter = 30.42 and Eleva3on = 808, so PA = 308’ 
•EX: Al3meter = 29.84 and Eleva3on = 808, so PA = 888’ 
ii.From Pressure Al3tude we can compute Density Al3tude (DA) 
a.DA: PA corrected for non-standard temperature (Directly related to airplane performance) 
b.DA = 120(Current Temperature - ISA Temperature) + PA 
•EX: Temp = 23oC, ISA = 15o C, PA = 308’ , so DA = 1,268’ 
•EX: Temp = 03oC, ISA = 15 o C, PA = 308’ , so DA = -1,132 
•This is a very good es3mate of DA, the equa3on is not perfect 
D.*Once we have PA, we can start at the temperature at the bomom of the chart and move up to the PA 
i.From there, we move straight across un3l we reach the next stage of the chart 
a.Once we reach the next step, follow the trend line and then move straight across 
E.This is done un3l we reach the performance number 
4.Determining the Required Performance is Acainable

i.The charts will provide performance for all phases of ﬂight 
ii.But, remember, the charts don’t make allowance for pilot proﬁciency or mechanical deteriora3on 
a.Does the airplane have problems that may limit performance? 
B.There is always the possibility of changing weather resul3ng in useless original calcula3ons 
i.Just because the plane will perform well now doesn’t mean it will perform well later 
ii.Plan ahead
