6.Exceeding Airplane Limita8ons 
A.Opera3ng Limita3ons are in Chapter 2 of the POH 
i.The limits here establish the boundaries in which the airplane can be safely operated 
ii.Adverse Eﬀects 
a.Amemp3ng to takeoﬀ or land without enough runway 
•Can result in a crash into an obstacle or over-running the runway also damaging the plane 
b.Amemp3ng to clear an obstacle that the airplane performance will not allow at a certain weight 
•Can result in crashing into the obstacle 
c.Not having enough fuel to reach the airport of intended landing 
•Can result in an emergency landing, or ditching 
d.Using the wrong type of fuel 
•Can result in detona3on, causing signiﬁcant damage to the engine, as well as engine failure 
e.Exceeding the structural/aerodynamic limits (overweight or outside CG limits) 
•Can result in airplane damage or structural failure 
•Airplane control may be hampered and stall speeds may be aﬀected 
f.Exceeding the maximum crosswind component (20 knots) 
•This will greatly increase the diﬃculty of the landing, possibly resul3ng in a crash 
•The airplane may not have the ability to stay aligned with the runway, resul3ng in a crash or 
depar3ng the landing surface

Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story

turned on anywhere at any 3me, the proper precau3ons and procedures must be followed for safety reasons. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Engine Star3ng discusses the safety precau3ons necessary when star3ng an airplane, the diﬀerent condi3ons 
which aﬀect star3ng the engine, as well as diﬀerent ways to start the engine. 
Why 
Proper engine star3ng is necessary for the safety of people and property, as well as to prevent engine

dangerous. It is very important to know the proper engine star3ng procedures and precau3ons. 
How: 
1.Safety Precau8ons 
A.Ensure the ramp area surrounding the airplane is clear of persons, equipment, and other hazards 
i.Be aware of what is in front of, and behind the airplane 
a.Check all direc3ons to ensure nothing is/will be in the vicinity of the propeller, or propeller blast

a.Mi3gate any hazard of blowing debris into persons or property

E.Keep one hand on the thromle to allow prompt response if rpm is excessively high or a hazardous

F.Common Error - Failure to use safety precau3ons related to star3ng 
G.Common Error - Failure to ensure proper clearance of the propeller 
i.Ensure the propeller area is clearance of any obstruc3ons (debris, people, obstacles, etc.) 
ii.Also verify that the area behind the aircrab, where debris is blown, is clear 
2.Atmospheric Condi8ons  
A.Cold Weather 
i.Low temperatures may cause a change in the viscosity of engine oils (they congeal, or become 
thicker), bameries may lose a higher percentage of their eﬀec3veness, and instruments may s3ck 
a.Preheat of the engine(s) (and cabin) before star3ng is desirable

b.Star3ng the Engine 
•In moderately cold weather, preheat may not be necessary

•Cold Engine Start Problems 
b.There is a tendency to overprime, which washes down cylinder walls and may result in

1.Also results in poor compression and consequently causes hard star3ng 
2.Aircrab ﬁres have been started by overpriming  
a.Have a ﬁreguard/ex3nguisher ready 
c.In a cold engine, icing over the sparkplug electrodes can cause problems 
1.When this happens, the engine only ﬁres a few revolu3ons and then quits 
a.There’s suﬃcient combus3on to cause some water in the cylinders, but not 
enough to heat them up 
b.The water condenses on the sparkplug electrodes, freezes to ice, and shorts 
them out 
c.Avoid prolonged idling  
i.Engines can quit during prolonged idling because suﬃcient heat is not 
produced to keep the plugs from fouling out 
ii.Frequently caused by iced-over spark plugs 
2.The only remedy is heat 
a.If a heater is not available, the plugs should be removed from the engine and

ii.Star3ng 
a.Prime the engine with fuel ﬁrst (over-priming can result in an aircrab ﬁre – AC 91-13.  AC 91-13 is 
s3ll available to read, but has been cancelled and incorporated into various other ACs.)

•As men3oned above, engines may quit during long idling since suﬃcient heat isn’t produced 
to keep the sparkplugs from fouling 
B.Hot Weather 
i.Follow the procedures in the POH 
a.Unless it is very hot, the normal start procedures will generally work 
•Use the hot start procedures, if necessary

priming

checklist to clear the excess fuel and start the engine 
ii.Vapor lock (fuel injected engines) 
a.Fuel delivery lines tend to be on the top of the engine, directly over the cylinder ﬁns 
b.Heat from the engine/outside can boil the fuel out of the fuel lines crea3ng vapor which can 
prevent the engine from star3ng

V. D.  Tax i i n g 
What 
Taxiing is the controlled movement of the airplane under its own power while on the ground. 
Why 
Since the airplane is moved by its own power between the parking area and runway, the pilot must 
thoroughly understand and be proﬁcient in taxi procedures. 
How: 
1.Taxiway Markings 
A.Used to transi3on from parking areas to the runway 
B.Taxiway Markings:  
i.Con3nuous Yellow Centerline stripe 
ii.Edge Markings 
a.If an edge marking is a con3nuous line, the shoulder is not intended for use by an airplane 
b.If it is a dashed marking, an airplane may use that por3on of the pavement 
iii.Holding Posi3on Marker (Hold Short Lines – Do Not cross un3l cleared to) 
a.Four yellow lines (two solid and two dashed), the solid lines are where the airplane is to hold 
b.When approaching the hold short lines from the dashed line side, you may cross without 
clearance 
•Clearance must be obtained to cross from the solid line side 
 
 
2.Taxi Clearance (AIM 4-3-18) 
A.Approval must be obtained prior to moving onto the movement area while tower is in opera3on 
B.A clearance must be obtained prior to crossing any runway; ATC will issue an explicit clearance for all 
runway crossings 
i.Any runway means any runway: ac3ve, inac3ve, open, closed, etc.  
C.When assigned taxi instruc3ons, ATC will specify: 
i.The runway or the point to taxi to 
ii.Taxi instruc3ons 
iii.Hold short instruc3ons or runway crossing clearances if the route will cross a runway 
a.This does not authorize the aircrab to enter or cross the assigned departure runway at any point 
D.When instruc3ons are received from the controller, always read back: 
i.The runway assignment 
ii.Any clearance to enter a speciﬁc runway 
iii.Any instruc3on to hold short of a speciﬁc runway 
E.Common Error – Hazards associated with the failure to comply with airport/taxiway surface marking, 
signals, and ATC clearances or instruc3ons 
i.Failure to comply can lead to incursions and accidents

ii.Always read all clearances back, and ensure understanding of airport signs and markings

3.How it works

•If s3ll too fast, rather than riding the brakes, allow the aircrab to accelerate, then use the

Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Everyone wants to sound like a real, professional pilot. This lesson will explain how we do that, while making 
you into a more professional pilot. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Radio communica3on is the communica3on between the pilot and diﬀerent ATC controllers throughout the 
phases of a ﬂight. 
Why 
Opera3ng in and out of a controlled airport, as well as in a good por3on of the airspace system, requires an 
aircrab have two-way radio communica3ons.  For this reason, a pilot should be knowledgeable of radio 
procedures.  Radio communica3ons is a cri3cal link in the ATC system. By understanding proper radio 
communica3on procedures, the link can be strong providing safer ﬂying for everyone. 
How: 
1.Procedure and Phraseology for Radio Communica8ons 
A.Understanding is the single most important thought in pilot-controller communica3ons 
i.It is essen3al that pilots acknowledge each radio call with ATC with the appropriate aircrab call sign  
ii.Brevity is important, but, if necessary, use whatever words will get your message across 
a.Know what you’re going to say before you say it 
iii.Good phraseology enhances safety and is the mark of a professional pilot 
a.The Pilot/Controller Glossary (link to the Glossary is under Publica3ons) is very helpful in 
learning what certain words/phrases mean 
B.Radio Technique 
i.LISTEN before you transmit 
ii.THINK before transmipng - Know what you want to say before you say it (write it down if needed) 
iii.Aber transmipng, wait a few seconds before calling again (The controller may be busy) 
iv.Be alert to the sound/lack of sounds in the receiver   
a.Check your volume, frequency, and make sure the microphone isn’t stuck on transmit 
v.Be sure you are within the performance range of your equipment and the ground sta3on equipment 
a.Remember higher al3tudes increase the range of VHF “line of sight” communica3ons 
C.Radio calls can be broken down into Who, Where, What: 
i.Who you are calling (Chicago Center) 
ii.Who you are (Diamond 4TS) 
iii.Where you are (10 miles South of _____) 
iv.What you want (Request ﬂight following, or whatever you want) 
D.Non-towered Airport Communica3on 
i.Radio calls at non-towered airports can be broken down into a similar format: 
a.Who you are  
•n-number 
b.Where you are

i.What is it?

•The diﬀerence between the high pressure below the wing and low pressure above the wing

VI.B. Traﬃc Pamerns 
 
i.Why is it dangerous? 
a.The rolling moments caused by the wake turbulence of a larger aircrab can be so strong that it 
exceeds the airplanes control authority 
•The rolling moments can be violent, and poten3ally unrecoverable 
b.If encountered at a close range, the turbulence generated by these vor3ces can damage aircrab 
components and equipment 
c.Wake turbulence can be encountered in any phase of ﬂight 
•Although usually strongest during departure, aircrab generate vor3ces during cruise ﬂight 
and on approach 
ii.Vortex Behavior 
 
a.Vor3ces are generated from the moment an aircrab leaves the ground, un3l it touches down 
b.Vor3ces tend to remain spaced a bit less than a wingspan apart, dribing with the wind, at 
al3tudes greater than a wingspan above the ground 
c.Vor3ces tend to sink at a rate of several hundred feet per minute, slowing their descent and 
diminishing in strength over 3me 
•When the vor3ces of large aircrab sink close to the ground (100-200’), they tend to move 
laterally over the ground at a speed of 2-3 knots 
a.A crosswind decreases the lateral movement of the upwind vortex and increases the 
movement of the downwind vortex

Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story

What 
The markings and signs used at airports, which provide direc3on and assist pilots in airport opera3ons.

How:

Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
The takeoﬀ is one of the most basic and exci3ng parts of ﬂying. Diﬀerent situa3ons regarding wind and 
weather, runway size and length, and the runway surface will provide diﬀerent challenges for every ﬂight. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A normal takeoﬀ is one in which the airplane is headed into the wind, or the wind is very light. Also, the 
takeoﬀ surface is ﬁrm, and of suﬃcient length to permit the airplane to gradually accelerate to normal lib-oﬀ 
and climb-out speed, and there are no obstruc3ons along the takeoﬀ path. 
While it is preferable to takeoﬀ into the wind, there will be many instances when circumstances dictate 
otherwise.  A crosswind takeoﬀ is a normal takeoﬀ with the only excep3on being that the airplane is no 
longer headed directly into the wind. 
Why

proﬁciency. It is essen3al for the pilot to be able to perform a safe and smooth takeoﬀ and have the ability to 
control the aircrab in varying condi3ons, star3ng with the basics. You need to be on your game while 
maneuvering close to the ground - takeoﬀs are, by deﬁni3on, performed at and near the ground. 
How: 
1.Normal Takeoﬀ 
A.General

VII.C. Sob-Field Takeoﬀ and Climb 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Have you ever got your car stuck oﬀ-roading? Why did it happen? So, what do we do when we have to takeoﬀ 
an airplane in oﬀ-road condi3ons? 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A takeoﬀ from a “sob” ﬁeld. Just like it says in the name, we are amemp3ng to takeoﬀ from a sob, oben 
uneven surface which could produce enough drag to prevent the airplane from reaching normal takeoﬀ 
speeds. 
Why 
Sob surfaces or long wet grass can reduce the aircrab's accelera3on so much during the takeoﬀ roll that 
adequate takeoﬀ speed might not be amained if normal takeoﬀ techniques were employed. As a maneuver, 
this will greatly improve your takeoﬀs, landings, and overall aircrab control. 
How: 
1.Overview 
A.Diﬀerences from a Normal Takeoﬀ: 
i.Hazards 
a.Reduced ability to accelerate 
•Taking oﬀ from a sob surface (sand, tall grass, snow, dirt, mud, etc.) reduces the airplane’s 
ability to accelerate during the takeoﬀ roll and may prevent the airplane from reaching 
adequate takeoﬀ speed using normal takeoﬀ techniques 
b.Poten3ally hazardous terrain 
•Even if the airplane could accelerate to takeoﬀ speed on the sob-ﬁeld, the high speed over 
rough, uneven terrain presents its own challenges 
a.Damage to the gear 
1.Debris as well as the high stress associated with uneven terrain 
b.Damage to the ﬂaps (more applicable to a low wing airplane) 
1.The longer the airplane stays on the ground, the more debris is thrown toward the 
ﬂaps  
c.Cartwheeling or ﬂipping 
1.If the nosewheel hit a hole during the takeoﬀ run the results could be catastrophic,

Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
The landing is the most diﬃcult, and most fun part of ﬂying. It doesn’t mamer how good the ﬂight was if the

Overview

What 
A normal approach and landing involves the use of procedures for what is considered a normal situa3on; that 
is, when engine power is available, the wind is light or the ﬁnal approach is made directly into the wind, the 
ﬁnal approach path has no obstacles, and the landing surface is ﬁrm and of ample length to gradually bring

Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story

Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A slip occurs when the bank angle of an airplane is too steep for the rate of turn. The airplane is in essence 
ﬂying sideways which increases drag as well as the rate of descent, without increasing the airspeed. 
Why 
Inten3onal slips are used to dissipate al3tude without increasing airspeed, and/or adjust airplane ground 
track during a crosswind. Inten3onal slips are especially useful in forced landings and in situa3ons where 
obstacles must be cleared during approaches to conﬁned areas. A slip can also be used as an emergency 
means of rapidly reducing airspeed in situa3ons where wing ﬂaps are inopera3ve or not installed. 
How: 
1.What is a Slip? 
A.A slip is a combina3on of forward movement and sideward movement 
i.The airplane is in fact ﬂying sideways resul3ng in a change in the direc3on the rela3ve wind strikes 
the plane 
B.Slips are characterized by 
i.An increase in drag 
a.Allows for the airplane to descend rapidly without an increase in airspeed 
ii.A corresponding decrease in airplane climb, cruise, and glide performance 
C.Posi3ve Sta3c Stability 
i.Most airplanes exhibit the characteris3c of posi3ve sta3c direc3onal stability and, therefore, have a 
natural tendency to compensate for slipping 
a.An inten3onal slip, therefore, requires deliberate cross-controlling ailerons and rudder 
throughout the maneuver to maintain the sideslip 
D.Two Types of Slips 
i.Forward Slip 
a.A forward slip is used to steepen the descent angle without excessively increasing the airspeed 
•Especially useful in forced landings and in situa3ons where obstacles must be cleared during 
approaches to conﬁned areas 
b.The wing on the side toward which the slip is to be made is lowered using the ailerons 
Simultaneously, the nose is yawed in the opposite direc3on by applying opposite rudder so that 
the longitudinal axis is at an angle to the original ﬂight path 
c.In a forward slip, the amount of slip, and therefore the sink rate, is determined by the bank angle 
•The steeper the bank, the steeper the descent 
ii.Sideslip 
a.A sideslip is used when landing with a crosswind to keep the aircrab aligned with the runway 
centerline and prevent dribing to either side of the centerline  
•In a sideslip, the longitudinal axis of the airplane remains parallel to the original ﬂight path 
a.Compared to a forward slip where the longitudinal axis is at an angle to the ﬂight path

Conclusion: 
Brief review of the main points 
The slip to a landing will increase the rate of descent, helping in many diﬀerent situa3ons. It is important to 
ensure the airplane maintains the desired ground track. In order to adjust the rate of descent we increase or 
decrease the bank angle and make the necessary rudder inputs to maintain our ground track. We can reach a 
point where we can no longer maintain the ground track; this is the Prac3cal Slip Limit. Also, ensure a smooth, 
gentle transi3on to landing to avoid sideloading and abrupt, violent maneuvering near the ground. To some 
extent, a sideslip can be used on almost every landing since the wind is rarely perfectly aligned with the runway. 
Use aileron to keep the aircrab over the runway, and rudder to align the longitudinal axis of the aircrab with the 
centerline of the runway.

Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Straight and level ﬂight is the basis of everything dealing with ﬂying. Every maneuver is based oﬀ a competent 
ability to maintain straight and level ﬂight. It is the ground work for your ﬂying abili3es, and as simple and 
boring as it sounds, it is extremely important. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Straight and level ﬂight is ﬂight in which a constant heading and al3tude are maintained. It is accomplished by 
making immediate and measured correc3ons for devia3ons in direc3on and al3tude from uninten3onal slight 
turns, descents, and climbs 
Why 
It is impossible to emphasize too strongly the necessity for forming correct habits in ﬂying straight and level.  
All other ﬂight maneuvers are in essence a devia3on from this fundamental ﬂight maneuver . It is not 
uncommon to ﬁnd a pilot whose basic ﬂying ability consistently falls just short of minimum expected 
standards, and upon analyzing the reasons for the shortcomings we discover that the cause is the inability to 
ﬂy straight and level properly. 
How: 
1.Flight Controls 
A.Axis of Rota3on

B.Pitch

•Overall Eﬀect

c.The pitching moment occurs about the CG

horizontal tail surface 
b.Forward pressure 
•Deﬂects the trailing edge of the elevator surface down 
a.Increases the camber, crea3ng more lib (less tail down force) 
•Overall Eﬀect 
b.Causes the tail to move upward and pitches the moment down 
c.The pitching moment occurs around the CG

Brief review of the main points 
Level ﬂight is maintained through pitch. We monitor pitch by keeping the reference point oﬀ the nose of the 
plane in the same place on the horizon, and referencing the al3meter and aptude indicator . Level ﬂight is 
controlled with elevator pressure.  Straight ﬂight is maintained through roll. We monitor bank by keeping an 
equal distance above (or below) each wing and the horizon, as well as maintaining a straight line between two 
points directly in front of the airplane.  These visual references are cross checked with the heading indicator as 
well as the aptude indicator . Trim is essen3al in relieving the pilot of the control pressures necessary to maintain 
level ﬂight. We should trim frequently and in small amounts in order to maintain straight and level ﬂight.

VIII.B. Level Turns
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Level turns sound boring and simple, but there is a lot more to turning than you might think, and a strong 
grasp on this will make many other maneuvers considerably easier . 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A level turn is a turn at a speciﬁed angle of bank in which al3tude and airspeed are maintained. 
Why 
The ability to understand and ﬂy a level turn is essen3al to the building of every pilot’s skill set. Level turns are 
the building blocks to many more diﬃcult maneuvers and will help the pilot in his or her control of the 
airplane. 
How: 
1.Flight Controls 
A.All four primary controls are used in coordina3on when making turns 
i.Ailerons - Bank the wings and determine the rate of turn at a given airspeed 
ii.Elevator - Moves the nose up or down in rela3on to the pilot, and perpendicular to the wings 
a.It sets the pitch aptude in the turn and “pulls” the nose around the turn 
iii.Rudder - Oﬀsets yaw eﬀects developed by the other controls (is not used to turn the airplane) 
iv.Thromle - Provides thrust which may be used to maintain airspeed during a turn 
2.How the Turn Works                          
A.Changing the direc3on of the wing’s lib to either side causes the airplane to be pulled that direc3on 
i.This is done by applying coordinated aileron and rudder to bank the airplane 
B.Lib 
i.In straight and level ﬂight, the total lib is ac3ng perpendicular to the wings and the Earth 
a.As the plane is banked, lib becomes the resultant of two components: 
•Ver3cal Component (VC) - Con3nues to act perpendicular to Earth and opposes gravity, or 
the weight of the airplane 
•Horizontal Component (HC) - Acts parallel to the Earth’s surface and opposes iner3a (or 
Centrifugal Force) 
b.The ver3cal and horizontal components act at right angles to each other (shown in the picture 
below); total lib acts perpendicular to the banked wings 
•The horizontal component of lib is what actually turns the airplane, not rudder

C.Adverse Yaw 
i.When the pilot deﬂects the ailerons to bank the

D.Overbanking Tendency

b.In a shallow banked turn, the diﬀerence in lib

What

2.Forces in the Climb 
A.Forces of Flight 
i.Summary 
a.In a climb, weight no longer acts perpendicular to the ﬂightpath

a.This causes an increase in total drag requiring an increase in thrust to balance the forces

IX.A. Steep Turns 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Steep turns - the ﬁrst really fun maneuver! Steep banks, you feel some G’s and you’re staring at the ground 
out the side window! 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
The steep turn maneuver consists of a constant al3tude turn in either direc3on, using a bank angle between 
45o to 60o (45o - Private, or 50o - Commercial). This will cause an overbanking tendency during which 
maximum turning performance is amained and rela3vely high load factors are imposed. 
Why 
Steep turns develop smoothness, coordina3on, orienta3on, division of amen3on, and control techniques 
necessary for the execu3on of maximum performance turns. The pilot also understands the eﬀects of the 
over banking tendency and how to counteract it. 
How: 
1.Maximum Performance Turn 
A.An airplane’s maximum turning performance is its fastest rate of turn and shortest radius of turn  
i.This changes with both airspeed and angle of bank 
a.The higher the airspeed, the bigger the radius 
b.The higher the bank angle, the smaller the radius 
B.In addi3on to other factors, the maximum bank angle is determined by the limi3ng load factor which can 
be maintained without stalling or exceeding the airplane’s structural limita3ons 
a.In most small airplanes the max bank is approx. 50o to 60o 
2.The Science Behind It 
A.What makes an airplane turn? 
i.As an aircrab banks lib is divided into a horizontal as well as a ver3cal component 
a.The horizontal component of lib pulls the aircrab through the turn 
b.The ver3cal component of lib must be increased in order to maintain al3tude 
 
B.Bank Angle, Load Factor and Stall Speed

IX.A. Steep Turns 
i.Basics 
a.As bank angle increases, the load factor increases and so does stall speed 
•Assuming level ﬂight 
•The opposite also applies – decreasing bank angle decreases load factor and stall speed 
ii.Load Factors 
a.As bank increases beyond 45o, the loads on the aircrab increase rapidly 
•At a 60o bank, a load factor of 2 Gs are imposed on the aircrab structure 
•At a 70o bank, a load factor of approximately 3 Gs are placed on the aircrab 
a.Most general avia3on airplanes are stressed for approximately 3.8 Gs 
b.Regardless of the airspeed or type of aircrab involved, a given angle of bank in a turn, during 
which al3tude is maintained, will always produce the same load factor 
•Ex: 60o of bank will always produce 2 G’s, irrespec3ve of airspeed, aircrab, power sepng, 
etc. 
iii.Stall Speed 
a.As we men3oned, increased bank leads to increased load factors, and increased load factor 
leads to an increased stall speed 
•The stall speed increases in propor3on to the square root of the load factor 
a.Ex: An aircrab will a normal stall speed of 50 knots in a 3G turn will stall at approximately 
85 knots  
iv.Thus, it’s very important to recognize and understand the rela3onship between bank angle and stall 
speed, especially in a steep turn 
C.Adverse Yaw 
i.In a turn, the downward deﬂected aileron (raised wing) produces more lib, and therefore more drag 
than the upward deﬂected aileron (lowered wing) 
a.This added drag yaws the airplane’s nose in the direc3on of the raised wing (opposite the turn) 
ii.Rudder is used to counteract adverse yaw 
a.The slower the aircrab and the larger the aileron deﬂec3on, the more rudder required to 
maintain coordina3on 
•At slower speeds the rudder is less eﬀec3ve

D.Torque Eﬀect (leb rolling tendency) 
i.Newton’s 3rd Law – every ac3on has an equal and opposite reac3on 
a.The internal engine parts and propeller are revolving in one direc3on (clockwise from the pilot’s 
perspec3ve), an equal force is trying to rotate the airplane in the opposite direc3on 
(counterclockwise, or leb, from the pilot’s perspec3ve) 
b.This force acts around the longitudinal axis, tending to make the airplane roll to the leb 
•The faster the engine/prop are spinning, the stronger the leb turning tendency 
ii.Torque Eﬀect in Turns 
a.Torque is based on the speed the engine/propeller are rota3ng  
•The higher the power sepng, the greater the turning tendency 
a.Takeoﬀ, for example, is when the turning tendency is most pronounced 
b.Most small aircrab combat the torque eﬀect in cruise ﬂight through trim tabs (whether adjusted 
in the cockpit by the pilot or via tabs mounted on the wings)  
•This is done to prevent having to hold right aileron pressure while cruising. Because of this, 
torque eﬀect is generally negligible during a steep turn 
a.Large changes in power would increase or decrease torque eﬀect and require 
corresponding aileron adjustments 
c.Leb Turn 
•Torque, as a leb rolling tendency, encourages a leb turn 
a.Large power changes would require the pilot to adjust aileron input to maintain the 
desired bank angle 
•Torque combined with the other leb turning tendencies can result in a skid in a leb turn 
b.Increase right rudder or reduce leb rudder to counteract the skid 
d.Right Turn 
•Torque, as a leb rolling tendency, discourages a right turn 
a.Large power changes would require the pilot to adjust aileron input to maintain the 
desired bank angle 
•Torque combined with the other leb turning tendencies can result in a slip in a right turn 
b.Increase right rudder or decrease leb rudder to counteract the slip 
E.Overbanking Tendency 
i.During any turn, the wing on the outside of the turn travels a longer path rela3ve to the wing on the 
inside of the turn 
a.As the radius of a turn becomes smaller, a signiﬁcant diﬀerence develops between these two 
paths. Although the outside wing is traveling a farther distance (larger circle) than the inside

IX.B. Steep Spirals 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
This can be a really cool maneuver, especially when combined with a power oﬀ 180o landing.  The ability to 
maintain a posi3on over the ground, while descending (as in an emergency landing) makes for a much more 
conﬁdent pilot. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A steep spiral is a constant gliding turn, during which a constant radius around a point on the ground is 
maintained similar to the turn around a point maneuver . 
Why 
The steep spiral improves pilot techniques for airspeed control, wind drib control, planning, orienta3on, and 
division of amen3on.  The steep spiral is not only a valuable ﬂight training maneuver, but it has prac3cal 
applica3on in providing a procedure for dissipa3ng al3tude while remaining over a selected spot in 
prepara3on for landing, especially for emergency forced landings. 
How: 
1.Rules 
A.Maintain an equal radius of turn around a point 
i.The radius should be such that the steepest bank will not exceed 60o 
a.Approximately ¼ mile is a good reference 
ii.Like turns around a point 
a.Adjust for changing tailwinds/headwinds 
B.Bank angle is increased as groundspeed increases and decreased as groundspeed decreases to maintain 
a consistent radius 
C.Enter on the downwind 
i.This will establish the steepest bank ini3ally since groundspeed is the highest at this point 
a.If the pilot entered on the upwind (slowest groundspeed) and rolled into 45o of bank, upon 
reaching the downwind leg (highest groundspeed) bank would have to be increased to 
excessively - by entering on the downwind, the pilot can establish the steepest bank angle at the 
beginning 
ii.This helps establish the radius to use throughout the spiral 
D.The spiral should be con3nued through three 360o spirals 
i.Suﬃcient al3tude must be amained 
a.The maneuver should not be con3nued below 1,500’ AGL unless performing an emergency 
landing in conjunc3on 
b.Triple the approximate al3tude lost per turn in your aircrab and add 1500’ to it to plan a 
minimum entry al3tude 
•Minimum al3tude = 1500’ AGL + 3 turns  
E.Clear the engine periodically while headed into the wind 
i.Opera3ng at idle for a prolonged period of 3me may result in excessive engine cooling or spark plug 
fouling 
ii.Clearing while facing into the wind minimizes any varia3on in groundspeed and radius of turn

iii.Maximum performance is degraded if power is not set to max 
a.Less power results in less al3tude, ensure maximum power is used 
iv.Maximum performance is degraded if the aircrab is not coordinated throughout the maneuver 
a.Uncoordinated ﬂight results in extra drag, decreasing performance  
Common Errors: 
•Improper pitch, bank, and power coordina3on during entry or comple3on 
•Uncoordinated use of ﬂight controls 
•Improper planning and 3ming of pitch and bank aptude changes 
•Factors related to failure in achieving maximum performance 
• A stall during the maneuver 
Conclusion: 
Brief review of the main points 
The chandelle is a maximum performance climbing 180o turn. During the ﬁrst half of the turn bank is held 
constant while pitch is constantly increased. Through the second half of the turn, pitch is held constant and bank 
is constantly decreased. Throughout the maneuver it is important to keep the airplane coordinated, especially as 
the speed of the airplane decreases.

What

rectangular area on the ground. 
Why

X.A. Rectangular Course 
4.Performing the Rectangular Course  
A.Prior to Entry 
i.*Pre-Maneuver Checklist - Lights ON; Fuel Pump ON; Mixture FULL RICH; Gauges GREEN 
ii.Clearing Turns 
iii.*Airspeed - 95 knots and trimmed for hands oﬀ, level ﬂight 
iv.Orienta3on - Orient yourself in rela3on to the wind, plan to enter on a 45o entry to the downwind 
B.The Maneuver 
i.Entry is made at a 45o to the downwind (like a traﬃc pamern) 
a.Upon reaching ½ to ¾ miles from the ﬁeld, turn to a downwind heading, parallel to the ﬁeld 
ii.Downwind Leg 
a.Since the airplane has a direct tailwind, no wind correc3on is needed 
•If the wind isn’t a perfect tailwind, point the airplane into the wind as necessary to maintain 
the ground track 
b.An3cipate and visualize the turn to the base leg 
•The turn:  
a.High roll rate 
b.Steepest bank transi3ons to medium bank 
c.Greater than 90o turn 
•Roll Rate 
d.A high roll rate is required to prevent the tailwind from pushing the aircrab away from 
the track 
•Bank 
e.Remember, as groundspeed changes during a turn, bank has to change with it to 
maintain the track 
1.At the beginning of the turn, the airplane has the strongest tailwind and therefore 
the highest groundspeed. Bank will be the steepest 
2.As the turn progresses, the tailwind transi3ons to a crosswind. Groundspeed is 
decreasing, therefore, bank will decrease as the airplane makes its way around the 
turn 
•Roll Out/Amount of Turn 
f.On the base leg, the crosswind will tend to push the aircrab away from the ﬁeld 
g.To compensate for the drib, the turn to the base leg will have to be more than 90o, and a 
crab will have to be established into the wind 
1.When rolling out onto this leg, the airplane will be turned slightly toward the ﬁeld/

4.The Basics 
A.The Maneuver 
i.The maneuver consists of crossing the reference line at a 90o angle (perpendicular) on a downwind, 
and immediately beginning a 180o, constant radius turn in one direc3on 
ii.The pilot should reference the airplane’s nose and wing3ps, and the ground references and adjust 
the rollout so that the airplane crosses the straight-line ground reference with the wings level, at the 
proper heading (opposite the entry heading), al3tude, and airspeed 
iii.As the airplane crosses the reference line, the pilot should immediately begin a 180o, constant radius 
turn in the opposite direc3on 
B.To maintain the constant radius for each turn, the pilot constantly adjusts roll rate and bank angle for the 
eﬀects of wind and changing groundspeed 
i.Roll Rate 
a.The rate of rolling in and out of the turn will need to be adjusted to prevent dribing in or out of 
the course  
•When the wind is from a direc3on that could push the airplane away from the reference line 
(and the aircrab has a high groundspeed), the rate of roll should be high/ 
a.Ex: Entering the maneuver on the downwind leg 
•When the wind is from a direc3on that could take the aircrab toward the reference line (and 
the aircrab has a lower groundspeed), the roll rate should be slow  
b.Ex: Star3ng the second turn, on the upwind leg 
ii.Bank Angle 
a.As groundspeed increases, bank angle will need to increases, and as groundspeed decreases, 
bank angle will need to decrease 
•For example, when star3ng the maneuver on the downwind (highest groundspeed), bank 
starts the steepest and is gradually shallowed as the aircrab turns into the wind and 
groundspeed decreases 
•The opposite occurs on the second turn as the headwind transi3ons back into a tailwind 
iii.Wind Correc3on Angle 
a.In addi3on to the rate of roll and bank angle, the pilot must also control the wind correc3on 
angle to maintain a constant radius 
•For example, if the pilot starts the maneuver with a leb turn, and the airplane is exactly 
crosswind, at the 90o point of the turn, with a crosswind requiring 10 o wind correc3on 
angle, the airplane would be ﬂying a heading that is 10o ahead when directly over the 90o 
ground reference point. In other words, to compensate for the crosswind and prevent the 
aircrab from being pushed away from the reference line, the ﬁrst 90 o track over the ground 
would result in a heading change of 100 o, and the last 90 o track over the ground would 
result in 80 o of heading change 
•In the second turn, to the right, the heading change would be the reverse. The ﬁrst 90o of 
turn would result in 80o of heading change, and the second 90o of turn would result in 100o 
of heading change 
b.The wind correc3on angle varies with the strength of the crosswind 
•The stronger the crosswind, the greater the wind correc3on angle required 
•The wind correc3on angle will increase from the start of the turn to the 90o point (max 
crosswind), and then decrease from the 90o point to the rollout

iii.Wind Correc3on Angle  
a.In addi3on to the rate of roll and bank angle, the pilot must also control the wind correc3on

result in a heading change of 100 o, and the second 90o track over the ground would result in

X.D. Eights on Pylons 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
The eights on pylons maneuver started in WWI. This maneuver was 
developed in order to maintain a constant view of a target, allowing the 
gunner to destroy a target. A more prac3cal applica3on now, is keeping the 
wing out of the way for aerial photography. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Eights on Pylons is an advanced maneuver in which the pilot’s amen3on is directed at maintaining a pivotal 
posi3on on a selected pylon, with minimum amen3on inside the cockpit. 
The maneuver itself involves ﬂying the airplane in a ﬁgure eight path around two selected points, or pylons, 
on the ground. However, no amempt is made to maintain a uniform distance from the pylon. Instead, the goal 
is to have an imaginary line that extends from the pilot’s eyes to the pylon. This line must be imagined to 
always be parallel to the airplane’s lateral axis. Along this line, the airplane appears to pivot as it turns around 
the pylon. In other words, if a taut string extended from the airplane to the pylon, the string would remain 
parallel to lateral axis as the airplane turned around the pylon. At no 3me should the string be at an angle to 
the lateral axis.  
Why 
The objec3ve of this maneuver is to develop the ability to maneuver the airplane accurately while dividing 
one’s amen3on between the ﬂight path and the selected points on the ground.  Eights on Pylons are 
extremely helpful in teaching, developing, and tes3ng subconscious control of the airplane. 
How: 
1.What is Pivotal Al8tude 
A.General Descrip3on 
i.A speciﬁc al3tude at which, for a given groundspeed, the projec3on of the visual reference line to 
the pylon appears to pivot 
a.Basically, the pivotal al3tude is the al3tude which keeps the pylon in the same posi3on on the 
window (or other aircrab reference, like the wing3p) as the aircrab turns around it 
•The al3tude varies with groundspeed 
•The reference line is parallel with the lateral axis of the airplane 
a.*Oﬀ the wing3p in the case of the DA20 
b.In a swept wing aircrab, there will be no wing reference, so the point has to be kept in 
the same posi3on on the window 
1.The same as keeping the pylon in the center of a target on the window  
ii.When an aircrab is turning at the pivotal al3tude, the wing3p appears to be ﬁxed to a single point in 
the landscape, but when at any height other than the pivotal al3tude, the wing 3p will appear to 
move across the landscape 
a.When an aircrab is turning at a height greater than the pivotal al3tude, which is the normal 
situa3on in ﬂight, the wing3p appears to move backward over the landscape 
b.When an aircrab is turning at a height less than pivotal al3tude (close to the ground) the wing3p 
appears to move forward over the landscape

2.The Basics 
A.Pivotal Al3tude is Based on Groundspeed 
i.As groundspeed increases, pivotal al3tude increases, and as groundspeed decreases, pivotal al3tude

a.The pivotal al3tude does not change with bank 
•Distance from the pylon aﬀects the angle of bank (more below) 
ii.Since the headings throughout the turns con3nually vary from directly downwind to directly upwind, 
the groundspeed will constantly change 
a.This will result in the pivotal al3tude varying throughout the maneuver 
•To adjust for this, the pilot climbs or descends to compensate for the changing groundspeed 
and to maintain the visual reference with the pylon 
•The change in al3tude will depend on how much the wind aﬀects groundspeed 
a.Strong winds create larger changes in al3tude than light winds 
b.No wind would result in no change in al3tude 
B.Maintaining the Pivotal Al3tude References 
i.Pitch  
a.As groundspeed decreases, the pivotal al3tude decreases  
•If no changes are made as the aircrab slows, we will be above the pivotal al3tude 
a.The wing will appear to move backward across the landscape (the point will move 
forward in rela3on to the wing)

reference line to the pylon 
b.When we descend, airspeed increases slightly, increasing pivotal al3tude 
1.In eﬀect, we descend to the lower pivotal al3tude, and the pivotal al3tude comes up 
to us 
•General Rule: If the point moves FORWARD, apply FORWARD pressure

c.Correc3ons and Wind Speed 
•Correc3ons are like tracking a VOR 
a.Once the correc3on is made (or an intercept angle is established), remove the correc3on

Brief review of the main points

Eights on Pylons is the most advanced and most diﬃcult of the low al3tude ﬂight training maneuvers. Because of

Acen8on

Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Slow ﬂight is ﬂight at a speed which any further increase in angle of amack or load factor, or reduc3on in 
power will cause an immediate stall. 
Why 
The aircrab performs and is controlled diﬀerently at slower airspeeds. Maneuvering during slow ﬂight 
demonstrates the ﬂight characteris3cs and degree of controllability of an aircrab near the cri3cal angle of 
amack. In normal opera3ons, the aircrab would not be ﬂown this close to the cri3cal AOA, but because the 
aircrab is ﬂown at higher angles of amack and slower airspeeds in many phases of ﬂight (takeoﬀ, landing, go-
around), understanding how the aircrab performs and is controlled at reduced speeds is essen3al, especially 
in the case the aircrab ends up slower than intended.  
How: 
1.What is Slow Flight 
A.Technically, slow ﬂight is any speed that is less than cruise speed, however, in pilot training, it can be 
broken down into two elements 
i.The establishment, maintenance of, and maneuvering of the aircrab at airspeeds and in 
conﬁgura3ons appropriate to takeoﬀs, climbs, descents, landing approaches and go-arounds 
a.i.e., phases of ﬂight other than cruise 
b.This descrip3on is most applicable to every day ﬂying 
ii.Flight at a speed which any further increase in angle of amack or load factor, or reduc3on in power 
will cause… an immediate stall (PTS deﬁni3on), or will result in a s3ll warning (ACS deﬁni3on) 
a.This descrip3on is what is used for the slow ﬂight maneuver  
b.Objec3ve is to understand the ﬂight characteris3cs and how the ﬂight controls feel near the 
cri3cal AOA

C.Weight 
i.The heavier the aircrab is, the more lib is necessary to maintain al3tude 
a.As more lib is required, the angle of amack required to maintain level ﬂight is increased 
•An increased angle of amack brings the aircrab closer to the cri3cal angle of amack, and 
therefore the stall speed will be reached sooner (at a higher airspeed) than if the aircrab 
were lighter 
ii.A heavier aircrab is more stable than a lighter aircrab (generally, the posi3on of the center of gravity 
has more eﬀect on the stability) 
a.It takes more force to move a heavier object than a lighter one, therefore outside forces, such as 
gusts, will have less of an eﬀect on the aircrab 
iii.Controllability 
a.Because a heavier aircrab is already at a higher angle of amack for a given airspeed, less pitch will 
be required to reach the cri3cal angle of amack 
b.The increased weight and stability may help in controlling the aircrab

Understanding the characteris3cs that aﬀect slow ﬂight and how to perform this maneuver is an extremely

control responses during ﬂight at slow speed (takeoﬀ, climb, landings and go-arounds) to maintain safe ﬂight, 
and avoid uninten3onal stalls.

XI.B. Power-On Stalls (Proﬁciency)
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Stalls can be in3mida3ng and frightening but understanding how they work and prac3cing them will make 
you more comfortable with them and a much safer pilot. A stall can occur at any airspeed, in any aptude, or 
any power sepng. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A stall occurs when the cri3cal angle of amack is exceeded. When this happens, the smooth airﬂow over the 
wing is disrupted resul3ng in a loss of lib and increased drag. Power on stalls (also known as departure stalls) 
are prac3ced to simulate stalls in the takeoﬀ and climb-out condi3ons and conﬁgura3on. 
Why 
Stalls in general are prac3ced to become familiar with an aircrab’s par3cular stall characteris3cs and to avoid 
pupng the aircrab into a poten3ally dangerous situa3on. Power-on stalls are essen3al to safety in the aircrab. 
It is important to understand how they happen, how to avoid them, and how to recover from them. 
How: 
1.Aerodynamics 
A.Why an Aircrab Stalls 
i.Basically… 
a.A stall occurs when the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing is disrupted and lib decreases 
rapidly 
•This happens when the wing exceeds its cri3cal angle of amack (AOA) 
a.The cri3cal AOA varies between aircrab, but is usually around 15-20o in a general 
avia3on aircrab 
b.Remember, AOA is the angle between the chord line of the wing and the rela3ve wind 
•A stall can occur at any airspeed, in any aptude, with any power sepng 
ii.More Speciﬁcally… 
a.Airﬂow Over the Wing 
•A certain amount of lib is generated by the diﬀerence in pressure between the top and 
bomom of the wing. This lib is dependent on the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing (A 
in the graphic below) 
•As AOA increases, the airﬂow over the top of the wing cannot maintain the smooth ﬂow and 
starts to burble and separate from the trailing edge (B in the graphic below) 
•As the AOA con3nues to increase, the separa3on point moves farther forward along the top 
of the wing hindering its ability to create lib, and leading to airﬂow separa3on and a stall (C 
in the graphic below) 
a.Thus, a stall occurs due to a rapid decrease in lib caused by the separa3on of the airﬂow 
from the wing’s surface

6.Recovery 
A.Basics: Disconnect, Pitch, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize, Conﬁgure (perform each step as appropriate) 
i.Disconnect the autopilot 
ii.Pitch nose down

B.Ailerons and Recovery 
i.Most general avia3on aircrab are designed to stall progressively outward from the wing root 
a.The wings are designed in this manner so that aileron control will be available at high AOA and 
give the airplane more stable stalling characteris3cs 
b.During the recovery, the return of lib begins at the 3ps and progresses towards the roots 
•Thus, ailerons can be used to level the wings 
ii.If the wing is fully stalled (ailerons included), using the ailerons can aggravate the stall 
a.EX: If the right wing dropped, and excessive aileron was applied to raise the wing, the right wing 
(aileron down) would produce a greater AOA and more (induced) drag 
•Increasing the AOA on an already stalled wing will aggravate the stall on that wing

•The increase in drag and aggravated stall on the low wing will yaw the aircrab in the

C.Rudder and Recovery 
i.The primary cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the cri3cal AOA while applying excessive or 
insuﬃcient rudder and, to a lesser extent, aileron. 
a.Therefore, it is important that the rudder be used properly during the entry and recovery 
ii.The primary use of rudder is to counteract any tendency of the airplane to yaw or slip 
iii.One wing will oben drop in a power-on stall 
a.Maintaining direc3onal control and coordinated ﬂight with the rudder is vital in avoiding a spin 
D.Common Errors During Recovery: 
i.Excessive al3tude loss or excessive airspeed during recovery 
a.Only lower the nose enough to break the stall, aber the stall is broken establish a climb 
b.Excessive speeds and nose low aptudes close to the ground are extremely hazardous 
ii.Poor stall recogni3on and delayed recovery  
a.Do not delay recovery, recover at the ﬁrst indica3on of stall (unless required otherwise by the 
ACS/PTS) - At slow airspeeds, in a descent, close to the ground any delay could be hazardous 
iii.Secondary stall during recovery 
a.Once the stall is broken, do not aggressively lib the nose to reestablish a climb as this can quickly 
result in a secondary stall 
b.Use smooth, controlled inputs; monitor performance to ensure the airplane is ready to climb 
iv.Rough and/or uncoordinated use of the ﬂight controls 
a.Just like in slow ﬂight, use smooth movements in controlling the airplane, nothing jerky 
b.A smooth controlled recovery is the goal, this will also help to avoid a secondary stall

•Improper pitch, heading, yaw, and bank control during straight ahead and turning stalls 
•Improper pitch, yaw, and bank control during turning stalls

•Failure to recognize the ﬁrst indica3ons of a stall 
•Failure to achieve a stall 
•Improper torque correc3on 
•Poor stall recogni3on and delayed recovery 
•Excessive al3tude loss or excessive airspeed during recovery 
•Secondary stall during recovery

XI.C. Power-Oﬀ Stalls (Proﬁciency)
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Stalls can be in3mida3ng/frightening but understanding how they work and prac3cing them will make you 
more comfortable with them, and a safer pilot. A stall can occur at any airspeed, in any aptude, or any power 
sepng. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A stall occurs when the cri3cal angle of amack is exceeded. When this happens, the smooth airﬂow over the 
wing is disrupted resul3ng in a loss of lib and increased drag. Power oﬀ stalls are prac3ced to simulate stalls in 
the landing and approach condi3ons and conﬁgura3on. 
Why 
Stalls in general are prac3ced to become familiar with an aircrab’s par3cular stall characteris3cs and to avoid 
pupng the aircrab into a poten3ally dangerous situa3on. Power-oﬀ stalls are essen3al to safety in the 
aircrab. It is important to understand how they happen, how to avoid them, and how to recover from them. 
How: 
1.Aerodynamics 
A.Why an Aircrab Stalls 
i.Basically… 
a.A stall occurs when the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing is disrupted and lib decreases 
rapidly 
•This happens when the wing exceeds its cri3cal angle of amack (AOA) 
a.The cri3cal AOA varies between aircrab, but is usually around 15-20o in a general 
avia3on aircrab 
b.Remember, AOA is the angle between the chord line of the wing and the rela3ve wind 
•A stall can occur at any airspeed, in any aptude, with any power sepng 
ii.More Speciﬁcally… 
a.Airﬂow Over the Wing 
•A certain amount of lib is generated by the diﬀerence in pressure between the top and 
bomom of the wing. This lib is dependent on the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing (A 
in the graphic below) 
•As AOA increases, the airﬂow over the top of the wing cannot maintain the smooth ﬂow and 
starts to burble and separate from the trailing edge (B in the graphic below) 
•As the AOA con3nues to increase, the separa3on point moves farther forward along the top 
of the wing hindering its ability to create lib and leading to airﬂow separa3on and a stall (C 
in the graphic below) 
a.Thus, a stall occurs due to a rapid decrease in lib caused by the separa3on of the airﬂow 
from the wing’s surface

D.Weight

ii.A lighter aircrab will stall at a slower airspeed 
a.The same as above, but the opposite. Less lib is required, and the AOA can be reduced (all other

E.Center of Gravity 
i.Forward Center of Gravity (CG) 
a.Increases the stall speed  
b.A forward center of gravity has the same eﬀect on stall speed as a heavier aircrab

c.The aircrab is also more controllable

increases drag, and thus the aircrab 
is slower for a given power sepng 
ii.Ab CG 
a.Decreases the stall speed 
b.An ab center of gravity has the same eﬀect on stall speed as a lighter aircrab 
•The farther ab the center of gravity moves, the lower the angle of amack has to be to

will stall at a lower speed 
c.Although the stall speed is lower, the aircrab is less controllable due to the shorter arm from the

•The elevator has a shorter arm to the CG, and thus produces less force making recovery 
more diﬃcult

c.Power is not essen3al to stall recovery, reducing the AOA is the only way of recovering 
d.Right rudder will be required to maintain coordina3on/heading 
•Use outside references - add rudder to keep the nose from yawing across the horizon 
v.Stabilize/establish the desired ﬂight path  
a.In this case, perform a go around and climb at the desired airspeed VY (VX if necessary) 
vi.Conﬁgure  
a.Once in a climb, conﬁgure the aircrab as necessary 
b.Same ﬂap and gear retrac3on procedure as a go around 
B.Ailerons and Recovery 
i.Most general avia3on aircrab are designed to stall progressively outward from the wing root 
a.The wings are designed in this manner so that aileron control will be available at high AOA and 
give the airplane more stable stalling characteris3cs 
b.During the recovery, the return of lib begins at the 3ps and progresses towards the roots 
•Thus, ailerons can be used to level the wings 
ii.If the wing is fully stalled (ailerons included), using the ailerons can aggravate the stall  
a.EX: If the right wing dropped, and excessive aileron was applied to raise the wing, the right wing 
(aileron down) would produce a greater AOA and more (induced) drag 
•Increasing the AOA on an already stalled wing will aggravate the stall on that wing 
•The increase in drag and aggravated stall on the low wing will yaw the aircrab in the 
direc3on of that wing and could result in a spin 
C.Rudder and Recovery 
i.The primary cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the cri3cal AOA while applying excessive or 
insuﬃcient rudder and, to a lesser extent, aileron 
a.Therefore, it is important that the rudder be used properly during the entry and recovery 
ii.The primary use of rudder is to counteract any tendency of the airplane to yaw or slip 
D.Common Errors During Recovery: 
i.Excessive al3tude loss or excessive airspeed during recovery 
a.Only lower the nose enough to break the stall, aber the stall is broken establish a climb 
b.Excessive speeds and nose low aptudes close to the ground are extremely hazardous 
ii.Poor stall recogni3on and delayed recovery  
a.Do not delay recovery, recover at the ﬁrst indica3on of stall (unless required otherwise by the 
ACS/PTS) - At slow airspeeds, in a descent, close to the ground any delay could be hazardous 
iii.Secondary stall during recovery 
a.Once the stall is broken, do not aggressively lib the nose to reestablish a climb as this can quickly 
result in a secondary stall 
b.Use smooth, controlled inputs; monitor performance to ensure the airplane is ready to climb 
iv.Rough and/or uncoordinated use of the ﬂight controls 
a.Just like in slow ﬂight, use smooth movements in controlling the airplane, nothing jerky

1.Aerodynamics of a Cross-Controlled Stall  
A.Situa3on

and the nose to drop. To compensate, the pilot inputs right aileron (opposite direc3on of the leb 
rudder – the aircrab is now cross controlled), and raises the nose with back elevator pressure 
a.The addi3onal leb roll is caused by the leb rudder input, and the diﬀerence in lib between the

maintain the pitch  
v.Suddenly, the aircrab rolls sharply leb, inverted (or even into a spin)

vii.Even with these inputs, the aircrab rolls further to the leb and accelerates its descent to the ground 
B.Why did this happen? 
i.A cross control stall occurs when the cri3cal AOA is exceeded with aileron pressure applied in one 
direc3on and rudder pressure in the opposite direc3on, causing uncoordinated ﬂight 
a.A cross-control stall can lead to a violent roll toward the inside wing, and/or a spin 
ii.Two Important Eﬀects of the Excessive Rudder in the Turn – 1. Opposite aileron which creates the

a.Opposite Aileron

right aileron)

stalled, pulling up only sends the aircrab to the ground faster

XI.E. Elevator Trim Stalls
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Applying full power with too much nose up trim (as in an approach to land) can have dire results if we don’t 
know how to deal with it. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
The elevator trim stall maneuver shows what can happen when full power is applied for a go around and 
posi3ve control of the airplane is not maintained. 
Why 
A situa3on like this could occur during a go-around procedure from a normal approach or immediately aber 
takeoﬀ. The objec3ve is to show the importance of making smooth power applica3ons, overcoming strong 
trim forces, maintaining posi3ve control of the airplane to hold safe ﬂight aptudes, and using proper and 
3mely trim techniques. It is impera3ve that a stall not occur during an actual go-around. 
How: 
1.Aerodynamics  
A.Why an Aircrab Stalls 
i.Basically… 
a.A stall occurs when the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing is disrupted and lib decreases 
rapidly 
•This happens when the wing exceeds its cri3cal angle of amack (AOA) 
a.The cri3cal AOA varies between aircrab, but is usually around 15-20o in a general 
avia3on aircrab 
b.Remember, AOA is the angle between the chord line of the wing and the rela3ve wind 
•A stall can occur at any airspeed, in any aptude, with any power sepng 
ii.More Speciﬁcally… 
a.Airﬂow Over the Wing 
•A certain amount of lib is generated by the diﬀerence in pressure between the top and 
bomom of the wing. This lib is dependent on the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing (A 
in the graphic below) 
•As AOA increases, the airﬂow over the top of the wing cannot maintain the smooth ﬂow and 
starts to burble and separate from the trailing edge (B in the graphic below) 
•As the AOA con3nues to increase, the separa3on point moves farther forward along the top 
of the wing hindering its ability to create lib and leading to airﬂow separa3on and a stall (C 
in the graphic below) 
a.Thus, a stall occurs due to a rapid decrease in lib caused by the separa3on of the airﬂow 
from the wing’s surface

b.The Cri3cal Angle of Amack/CLMAX

good. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A secondary stall is a stall that occurs aber a recovery from a preceding stall. 
Why 
The loss of al3tude associated with a single stall can be poten3ally hazardous. By stalling the aircrab a second 
3me while recovering from the ﬁrst stall, the al3tude loss is ampliﬁed and the second stall may be more 
aggressive. Learning the proper stall recogni3on and recovery procedures and seeing/demonstra3ng a 
secondary stall will allow the pilot to safely recover the ﬁrst 3me and not aggravate the situa3on. 
How: 
1.Aerodynamics  
A.Why an Aircrab Stalls 
i.Basically… 
a.A stall occurs when the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing is disrupted and lib decreases 
rapidly

a.The cri3cal AOA varies between aircrab, but is usually around 15-20o in a general 
avia3on aircrab 
b.Remember, AOA is the angle between the chord line of the wing and the rela3ve wind 
•A stall can occur at any airspeed, in any aptude, with any power sepng 
ii.More Speciﬁcally… 
a.Airﬂow Over the Wing 
•A certain amount of lib is generated by the diﬀerence in pressure between the top and 
bomom of the wing. This lib is dependent on the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing (A 
in the graphic below) 
•As AOA increases, the airﬂow over the top of the wing cannot maintain the smooth ﬂow and 
starts to burble and separate from the trailing edge (B in the graphic below) 
•As the AOA con3nues to increase, the separa3on point moves farther forward along the top 
of the wing hindering its ability to create lib, and leading to airﬂow separa3on and a stall (C 
in the graphic below) 
a.Thus, a stall occurs due to a rapid decrease in lib caused by the separa3on of the airﬂow 
from the wing’s surface

XI.G. Spins
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Who WANTS to do a spin? Most people are scared of them, but understanding them will help in avoiding 
them and remove some of the fear . 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A spin is an aggravated stall that results in what is termed “autorota3on,” wherein the airplane follows a 
downward corkscrew path. 
Why 
Without an understanding of spins and the proper procedures to recover from them the pilot could be put in 
an impossible situa3on. Understanding spins will also increase conﬁdence and reduce the anxiety associated 
with spins. 
How: 
1.Spins and Anxiety 
A.Spins are scary 
i.A common percep3on to those unfamiliar with avia3on is that a spin is a death sentence 
ii.They’re scary even to a lot of pilots, BUT we’re going to set you up for success with knowledge and 
training 
a.In order to get into a spin, you have to stall the aircrab 
b.Through your training, the intent is that you never uninten3onally encounter a stall, but in the 
case that you do, you’re conﬁdent and capable of recovering 
c.From there, the intent is that you’re so well trained that even if you do uninten3onally 
encounter a stall, you never encounter a spin 
d.And, in the unlikely event that the ﬁrst two lines of defense fail, you will also know how to 
recover from a spin 
iii.Knowledge and training can remove the anxiety and make you a far safer and competent pilot 
2.Aerodynamics of a Spin 
A.Requirements for a Spin  
i.A spin occurs when the aircrab’s wings exceed their cri3cal AOA (stall) with a sideslip, or yaw, ac3ng 
on the airplane 
a.There are two requirements for a spin: 
•A stall 
•Yaw 
a.Can be for any reason - Incorrect rudder applica3on, adverse yaw, engine/propeller 
eﬀects, wind shear, wake turbulence, etc. 
b.The yaw can occur at, or beyond the actual point of stall 
B.Basically… 
i.In a spin, the inboard, lower wing is more stalled than the outboard wing, which creates an 
autorota3on, or rolling, yawing, and pitching mo3on around the ver3cal axis of the aircrab 
C.Speciﬁcally… 
i.When the aircrab stalls, one wing drops (the wing will drop in the direc3on of the yaw)

XI.G. Spins
a.Although both wings are stalled… 
•The wing that drops has an increasing angle of amack (more stalled) 
a.Lib decreases and drag increases on this wing 
•And, the rising wing has a decreasing AOA (less stalled)  
b.Lib increases and drag decreases on this wing 
ii.The autorota3on results from the unequal angle of amack on the airplane’s wings 
a.The diﬀerence in lib between the wings results in the rolling ac3on 
b.The diﬀerence in drag between the wings results in the yawing ac3on 
iii.The load factor during a spin varies with the spin characteris3cs of each aircrab, but is usually found 
to be slightly above the 1G of level ﬂight. There are two reasons for this: 
a.Airspeed in a spin is very low, usually within 2 knots of the unaccelerated stall speed 
b.An aircrab pivots, rather than turns, while it is in a spin 
D.There are 4 Phases of a Spin 
i.Entry Phase 
a.The pilot inten3onally or accidentally provides the elements for the spin (stall + yaw)

XI.G. Spins
a.Occurs when the airplane’s angular rota3on rate, airspeed, and ver3cal speed are stabilized in a 
ﬂightpath that is nearly ver3cal 
•The spin is in equilibrium – the airplane’s aptude, angles, and self-sustaining mo3ons about 
the ver3cal axis are constant or repe33ve, or nearly so 
iv.Recovery Phase 
a.Occurs when rota3on ceases and the AOA of the wings is decreased below the cri3cal AOA 
3.Rela8onship of Various Factors to Spins (Very similar to the informa3on in the Stall lessons since a stall leads 
to a spin) 
A.Conﬁgura3on 
i.Flaps – will generally increase the libing ability of the wings and therefore decrease stall speed 
v.Gear – the eﬀects of gear can vary based on the aircrab design and characteris3cs 
B.Weight 
i.As the weight of the aircrab is increased, the stall speed increases 
a.Remember, to maintain al3tude lib must equal weight 
b.So, the greater the weight, the greater the lib required 
c.A higher AOA is required to generate the lib (all other factors remaining the same) 
d.The higher AOA puts the aircrab closer to the cri3cal angle of amack, and therefore the aircrab 
will stall at a higher speed  
ii.A lighter aircrab will stall at a slower airspeed 
a.The same as above, but the opposite. Less lib is required, and the AOA can be reduced (all other 
factors remaining the same), lowering the stall speed 
C.Center of Gravity (CG) 
i.Forward Center of Gravity (CG) 
a.Increases the stall speed  
b.A forward center of gravity has the same eﬀect on stall speed as a heavier aircrab 
•The farther forward the center of gravity moves, the higher the angle of amack has to be to 
compensate for the extra load imposed by the tail (see picture) 
•Due to the higher angle of amack, the aircrab is closer to the cri3cal angle of amack and 
therefore will stall at a higher speed 
c.The aircrab is also more controllable due to the longer arm from the CG to the elevator, 
improving the stall and spin recovery 
capabili3es 
•Addi3onally, the farther forward the 
CG, the greater the tendency for the

Introduc8on: 
Acen8on

Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Stalls entered from ﬂight situa3ons that impose excessive maneuvering loads on the airplane. Situa3ons such 
as steeps turns, pull-ups, or other abrupt changes in ﬂightpath. 
Why 
Stalls which result from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more rapid, or severe, than the unaccelerated stalls, 
and because they occur at higher than normal airspeeds, and/or may occur at lower than an3cipated pitch 
aptudes, they may be unexpected.  
How: 
1.Aerodynamics of an Accelerated Maneuver Stall 
A.Why an Aircrab Stalls 
i.Basically… 
a.A stall occurs when the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing is disrupted and lib decreases 
rapidly 
•This happens when the wing exceeds its cri3cal angle of amack (AOA) 
a.The cri3cal AOA varies between aircrab, but is usually around 15-20o in a general 
avia3on aircrab 
b.Remember, AOA is the angle between the chord line of the wing and the rela3ve wind 
•A stall can occur at any airspeed, in any aptude, with any power sepng 
ii.More Speciﬁcally… 
a.Airﬂow Over the Wing 
•A certain amount of lib is generated by the diﬀerence in pressure between the top and 
bomom of the wing. This lib is dependent on the smooth airﬂow over the top of the wing (A 
in the graphic below) 
•As AOA increases, the airﬂow over the top of the wing cannot maintain the smooth ﬂow and 
starts to burble and separate from the trailing edge (B in the graphic below) 
•As the AOA con3nues to increase, the separa3on point moves farther forward along the top 
of the wing hindering its ability to create lib, and leading to airﬂow separa3on and a stall (C 
in the graphic below) 
a.Thus, a stall occurs due to a rapid decrease in lib caused by the separa3on of the airﬂow 
from the wing’s surface

XII.E. Recovery from Unusual Flight Aptudes 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
On July 16, 1999, JFK Jr . was killed along with his wife and sister-in-law, when the aircrab he was pilo3ng 
crashed into the Atlan3c Ocean. Kennedy had 310 hours of ﬂight experience, including 55 hours of night ﬂying 
and 36 hours in the high-performance Piper Saratoga. He had completed about half of an instrument training 
course. The NTSB inves3ga3on found no evidence of mechanical malfunc3on and determined that the 
probable cause was the pilot's failure to maintain control of the airplane during a descent over water at night, 
which was a result of spa3al disorienta3on (or, not recovering properly from an unusual aptude). Factors in 
the accident were haze, and the dark night. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
An unusual aptude is an airplane aptude not normally required for instrument ﬂight.  
Why 
Without proper recovery training on instrument interpreta3on and aircrab control, a pilot can quickly 
aggravate an abnormal ﬂight aptude into a poten3ally fatal accident.

XIII.A. Emergency Approach and Landing 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Understanding the elements behind a properly executed emergency approach and landing could be the 
diﬀerence between a safe sob ﬁeld landing and a dangerous, poorly performed crash. 
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
A simulated emergency landing occurs when the power is pulled, simula3ng a lost engine, and the pilot must 
run the checklist to amempt to restart the engine while properly conﬁguring the airplane for an approach and 
landing usually in a nearby ﬁeld. 
Why 
To develop accuracy, judgment, planning, technique, and conﬁdence when limle or no power is available. 
How: 
1.ABC - Aviate, Best Landing Spot, Checklists 
A.*AVIATE: The ﬁrst reac3on should be to immediately establish the best glide airspeed (73 KIAS) and ﬂy 
the airplane 
i.The most important priority is to ﬂy the airplane 
ii.Establish and maintain the best glide speed 
a.Varia3ons in air speed nullify accuracy in judgment of gliding distance/landing spot 
b.Eagerness to get down is one of the most common faults during simulated emergency landings 
•Pilots forget about speed and arrive at the edge of the ﬁeld too fast for a safe landing 
•Too much speed is just as dangerous as too limle  
iii.Common Error - Improper airspeed control 
a.Airspeeds other than the best glide airspeed result in diminished glide performance 
b.Know the general pitch aptude required for the best glide speed 
•Although this aptude can vary based on weight, CG, etc., start there and make small 
adjustments 
•Trim the airplane to maintain the speed and reduce workload in a busy situa3on  
c.If airspeed is too fast, gently raise the nose, allow airspeed to semle and readjust/re-trim 
d.If airspeed is too slow, gently lower the nose, allow airspeed to semle and readjust/re-trim  
B.BEST Landing Spot: Select the best landing spot and immediately turn toward it 
i.The pilot’s choice of emergency landing sites is governed by: 
a.The route selected during preﬂight planning 
b.The height above the ground when the emergency occurs 
c.Excess airspeed (excess airspeed can be converted into distance and/or al3tude) 
ii.If possible, ﬁnd a close by airport 
a.If GPS is available, use the Nearest page and make a decision based on glide speed as to whether 
or not the airport can be reached 
•*Glide ra3on is 11:1 (DA20) –  ~2 mile glide for every 1,000’ AGL (lose about 500’ per mile) 
iii.If an airport is not available or prac3cal, select a ﬁeld that is within glide distance  
a.Check in front, behind, and to BOTH sides of the airplane 
b.Preferably hard packed, long, smooth, and with no obstacles, especially at the approach end

A.The generator / alternator is the cause of most electrical system failures (indicated on the ammeter) 
i.Once the generator goes oﬄine, the only electrical source remaining is the bamery (3me limited) 
B.Electrically powered gear and ﬂaps use up power at rates much greater than most other equipment

i.Concentrate on ﬂying the plane, an open door seldom compromises the ability of the plane to ﬂy

iii.Don’t release the seatbelt to amempt to reach the door, leave the door alone, land, then close it 
iv.Most doors will not stay open, they will usually bang open then semle par3ally closed 
a.A slip toward the door may open it wider, and a slip away may push it closed 
10.Inopera8ve or “Runaway” Trim 
A.Grip the controls and maintain control of the plane while disengaging the electric trim system 
i.Disengage bumon, circuit breaker, etc. 
B.If the reason for the runaway trim is obvious and has been resolved, engage the breaker 
11.Flap Malfunc8on 
A.Total Flap Failure (no ﬂap approach and landing) 
i.Requires substan3ally more runway than normal (as much as 50% more)

iii.A wider, longer pamern may be necessary  
iv.Tend to ﬂoat during roundout (don’t force the plane onto the ground) 
B.Asymmetric (Split) Flap 
i.A situa3on in which one ﬂap deploys / retracts while the other remains in posi3on 
ii.Indicated by a roll toward the wing with the least ﬂap deﬂec3on 
iii.Countered with opposite aileron 
a.Yaw caused by the addi3onal drag on the extended ﬂap side requires opposite rudder 
b.Almost full aileron may be necessary at reduced airspeeds to maintain wings level 
•Do not amempt to land with a cross-wind from the side of the deployed ﬂap 
iv.Be aware of the diﬀering stall speeds of each wing 
a.The wing with the retracted ﬂap will stall earlier - possible cross-controlled stall condi3on 
v.Approach and landing should be ﬂown at a higher-than-normal airspeed 
12.Pressuriza8on Malfunc8on 
A.Descend or use supplemental oxygen 
B.Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression

Brief review of the main points 
Understanding diﬀerent emergencies and how to deal with them is obviously important as you will always be 
prepared and be able to react quickly in the event one of these emergencies occurs.

•The problem is indicated by a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least ﬂap deﬂec3on 
•Countering

11.Flap Malfunc8on 
A.Total Flap Failure 
•This will necessitate a no ﬂap approach and landing 
•This will require substan3ally more runway than normal (as much as 50% more depending on 
the aircrab – reference the POH performance) 
•The airplane must be ﬂown in a rela3vely nose-high aptude as compared to ﬂaps extended 
•This can make the runway diﬃcult to see 
•A wider, longer pamern may be necessary to avoid diving to lose al3tude and building up 
airspeed 
•The airplane will tend to ﬂoat considerably during roundout 
•If only ﬂaps are unavailable, raise the approach airspeed 10 knots and maintain a ﬂat approach angle 
•This is a general recommenda3on and not from the Cessna 172 POH 
B.Asymmetric (Split) Flap 
•A situa3on in which one ﬂap deploys/retracts while the other remains in posi3on 
•The problem is indicated by a pronounced roll toward the wing with the least ﬂap deﬂec3on 
•Countering 
•Countered with opposite aileron 
•The yaw caused by the addi3onal drag on the extended ﬂap side will require opposite rudder 
•Aileron and opposite rudder results in a crossed control situa3on 
•Almost full aileron may be necessary at the reduced airspeed to maintain wings level 
•Therefore, do not amempt to land with a cross-wind from the side of the deployed ﬂap 
a.The addi3onal roll control to counteract the cross-wind may not be available 
•Be aware of the diﬀering stall speeds of each wing 
•The wing with the retracted ﬂap will stall much earlier - possible crossed control stall condi3on 
•Approach and landing should be ﬂown at a higher than normal airspeed 
12.Pressuriza8on Malfunc8on 
A.Descend or use supplemental oxygen 
•Hypoxia is the primary danger of decompression

XIII.C. Emergency Equipment and Survival Gear 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
Would you want to crash land in the desert with a life rab, life preserver, warm clothes and an average water 
supply as your survival equipment? Or, wouldn’t you rather have survival gear tailored to the ﬂight you are 
taking? We want to be properly prepared for an emergency landing.  
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
Emergency equipment and survival gear refers to the equipment that should be carried onboard an airplane 
based on the ﬂight being taken to aid in survival and rescue opera3ons. 
Why 
By carrying and understanding the use of survival equipment tailored to your ﬂight you will greatly increase 
chances of rescue and survival. 
How: 
1.Appropriate Equipment and Gear 
A.For ﬂight over uninhabited land areas, it is wise to take and know how to use survival equipment for the 
type of climate and terrain 
B.A survival kit should provide sustenance, shelter, medical care and a means to summon help 
C.Consider the terrain, the climate/season, and type of emergency communica3on equipment needed 
i.Mountainous terrain in December requires diﬀerent survival gear than coastal ﬂying in August 
ii.Flying over the Midwest US poses diﬀerent threats than a coastal ﬂight 
iii.If a forced landing occurs at sea, chances for survival are governed by the degree of crew proﬁciency 
in emergency procedures and by the availability and eﬀec3veness of water survival equipment 
D.General Items to consider 
E.More speciﬁc items should be considered based on the type of ﬂight 
i.Ex: Life vests and a rab when ﬂying over water 
F.Think outside the box. What parts of the airplane/baggage could be used for survival? For example, the 
aircrab cover could be used for shelter, warmth, etc. 
2.Equipment Use and Care 
A.Onboard emergency equipment can oben consist of an ELT , a ﬁre ex3nguisher, emergency axe, and the 
survival gear you have packed 
B.ELT 
i.Purpose - transmit a downed aircrab’s loca3on for search and rescue personnel 
a.Broadcast on emergency frequencies of 121.5 and 243.0 (no longer monitored by satellite) and 
406 MHz on newer ELTs 
i.First Aid Kit and Field Medical Guide vi.Matches
ii.Flashlight and bameries vii.Shelter
iii.Food and Water viii.Signaling Device

a.In the case of some aircrab, the axe is used to cut through a por3on of the fuselage 
b.An axe is also a great addi3on to your survival gear 
iii.Servicing – Ensure the axe is onboard and properly mounted, and inspected as required  
iv.Storage – The axe should be stored in its mount as the manufacturer intends 
E.Survival Gear 
i.Purpose – Used for survival (food, water, shelter, warmth, etc.) 
ii.Opera3on/Use – The opera3on/use will vary by equipment. Use based on the instruc3ons  
iii.Servicing – Verify the equipment is in good working order and does not need replaced, cleaned, etc. 
a.Ensure electronic equipment (GPS, phone, addi3onal ELT , etc.) is in good working order and 
properly charged/ready for use 
b.Adjust the contents of the survival gear based on the trip, weather, terrain, etc. 
iv.Storage – Store the gear safely and accessibly on the airplane  
Conclusion: 
Brief review of the main points

XIII.D. Emergency Descent 
Instructor Notes:  
Introduc8on: 
Acen8on 
Interes3ng fact or amen3on-grabbing story 
This maneuver is a lot of fun to prac3ce, partly because there is not a lot too it, but also because the airplane 
is put in a very nose low aptude and is descending very fast. You’re dive bombing the ground.  
Overview 
Review Objec3ves and Elements/Key ideas 
What 
An emergency descent is a maneuver for descending as rapidly as possible to a lower al3tude, or to the 
ground for an emergency landing. 
Why 
The need for this maneuver may result from an uncontrollable ﬁre, a sudden loss of cabin pressuriza3on, or 
any other situa3on demanding an immediate and rapid descent. 
How: 
1.General 
A.Objec3ve 
i.To descend as soon and as rapidly as possible, within the structural limita3ons of the airplane 
B.Situa3ons 
i.Fire, smoke, loss of cabin pressuriza3on, or any other demanding situa3on (medical, injury, etc.) 
ii.Common Error - The consequences of failing to iden3fy reason for execu3ng an emergency descent 
a.If an emergency descent is necessary and not executed, the situa3on can become very 
dangerous, and unrecoverable 
•A ﬁre can grow/spread quickly –oben considered the most threatening hazard in an airplane 
•In the case of decompression, symptoms of hypoxia can set in 
C.Follow the procedures outlined in the Emergency Procedures sec3on of the POH 
2.The Maneuver 
A.Prior to the Maneuver 
i.Clear the area visually 
a.Thoroughly clear the area and broadcast inten3ons to alert other aircrab 
b.Ensure it is clear below the aircrab – turns are likely necessary, especially in low wing aircrab 
c.Common Error - Improper use of clearing procedures for ini3a3ng the emergency descent 
ii.*Pre-Maneuver Checklist: Fuel Pump ON, Mixture RICH, Lights ON, Gauges GREEN 
B.Procedure 
i.Reduce power to idle 
ii.Extend the ﬂaps and gear as required by the manufacturer  
a.Provides maximum drag to make increase the rate of descent, without excessive airspeed 
b.Common Error - Improper use of the prescribed emergency checklist to verify accomplishment 
of procedures for ini3a3ng the emergency descent 
•Follow the POH 
•If the airplane is not conﬁgured correctly, the rate of descent may be less than desired and/
or the airplane could be structurally damaged (exceeding airspeeds or load factors) 
•For example, leaving the ﬂaps up could decrease the rate of descent/increase the airspeed, 
poten3ally exceeding limita3ons (VNE), and overstressing the airplane during recovery

XIII.D. Emergency Descent 
iii.Put the nose down to maintain the maximum allowable airspeed based on the procedure 
a.*Nose down pitch is approximately 12o, but may be adjusted based on the conﬁgura3on 
b.This speed may vary based on ﬂaps used, the nature of the emergency, and turbulent condi3ons  
•Never exceed VNE or VFE and always maintain posi3ve control of the airplane 
•In an engine ﬁre, a high speed descent could blow out the ﬁre, however, weakening of the 
structure is a concern, and a low airspeed would result in less airframe stress

iv.As the nose is lowered, begin a 90o leb turn at 30-45o of bank

iv.Re-trim the aircrab and adjust/lean the mixture as necessary 
v.Common Error - Improper procedures for recovering from an emergency descent

b.Avoid overstressing the airplane with an aggressive level oﬀ

ini3a3ng the emergency descent

Conclusion: 
Brief review of the main points 
An emergency descent is used in a situa3on where al3tude must be lost quickly in order to make a landing as 
soon as possible. If possible, the manufacturer’s procedures should be followed. The airplane is put into a 
conﬁgura3on which will allow for the maximum descent rate. Recovery should be smooth and controlled as 
straight and level cruise ﬂight is reestablished.
